0.title: Waiting for His Son from Heaven
0.overview:
The message. First Thessalonians is a letter of hope to a young church under pressure. Its members had recently “turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God, and to wait for his Son from heaven” (1:9–10); now they were suffering for it, and some had died. Paul assures them that the gospel they received was God’s own word, that suffering is no sign God has left them, and that believers who have died are not lost: the Lord will come, the dead in Christ will rise, “and so we will always be with the Lord” (4:17). Until then they are to live holy, loving, steady lives. This is not vague optimism but a sure hope grounded in the resurrection, and it changes how believers grieve, work, treat their bodies and face the future.

Background: the writer. The letter comes from Paul, Silvanus (the Silas of Acts) and Timothy (1:1), though Paul’s own voice breaks through (2:18), and scholars of almost every school accept that he wrote it. He wrote from Corinth, probably about AD 50–51, soon after Timothy had rejoined him there (3:6; Acts 18:5); an inscription at Delphi dating Gallio’s term in Corinth (Acts 18:12) makes this one of the surest dates in the New Testament. Unless Galatians came first, it is the earliest of Paul’s letters we have, and perhaps the oldest book of the New Testament. A few scholars think the hard words about those Jews who opposed the gospel (2:14–16) were added later, but no manuscript lacks them; they speak of the persecutors, not of a race, and Paul, himself a Jew, sets the churches of Judea before the Thessalonians as their example.

Thessalonica. Thessalonica (modern Thessaloniki, in northern Greece), named after a half-sister of Alexander the Great, was a port on the Aegean and lay on the Via Egnatia, the great Roman road running east from the Adriatic (see Roads and Travel), so news spread from it quickly: “your faith in God has gone forth everywhere” (1:8). It was the capital of the Roman province of Macedonia and a free city that governed itself through its own magistrates, the “city authorities” of Acts 17:6. It honoured Rome and its rulers warmly, alongside the gods of Greece and Egypt. Some of the letter’s words would have rung there. A ruler’s “coming” (parousia) was his official visit, when leading citizens went out to “meet” him and escort him in, and Rome boasted of bringing peace and security. Paul’s readers learned that the true Lord’s coming lay ahead, and that the world’s “peace and security” would not stand on that day (5:3).

Paul and the church there. Paul came about AD 49 or 50, on his second journey, fresh from beatings and prison at Philippi (2:2; Acts 16:22–24), and for three Sabbaths reasoned in the synagogue that the Christ had to suffer and rise (Acts 17:2–3). Some Jews believed, with “a great many of the devout Greeks and not a few of the leading women” (Acts 17:4), God-fearers from the synagogue; but most of the church had come straight from idols (1:9). He probably stayed some weeks longer, working night and day at his trade (2:9) while the Philippians sent him help more than once (Philippians 4:16). Then jealous opponents roused a mob, which dragged his host Jason before the magistrates, charging that the missionaries “are all acting against the decrees of Caesar, saying that there is another king, Jesus” (Acts 17:7). The believers sent Paul and Silas away by night, leaving a church that was very young, untaught on much, and already under attack from “your own countrymen” (2:14).

What prompted the letter. Paul tried again and again to return, “but Satan hindered us” (2:18), so from Athens he sent Timothy back (3:1–2). Timothy returned with good news of their faith and love (3:6), and this letter is Paul’s overflowing answer. It also meets needs Timothy reported. Someone, it seems, was painting Paul as one more travelling preacher who flattered people for money and ran when it got hard (2:1–12). Converts from paganism needed teaching on sexual holiness, against the habits of their world (4:1–8). Some were neglecting their work (4:11–12; 5:14). And the death of believers had raised a grief Paul had not had time to address: would those who died before the Lord came miss his coming (4:13–18)?

How the letter makes its case. Chapters 1–3 look back; chapters 4–5 look ahead. Chapter 1 thanks God for the Thessalonians’ “work of faith and labor of love and steadfastness of hope” (1:3), a triad that appears here before 1 Corinthians 13, and for the gospel that came “not only in word, but also in power and in the Holy Spirit and with full conviction” (1:5). Chapter 2 recalls how Paul lived among them, gentle “like a nursing mother” (2:7), yet urging them “like a father with his children” (2:11) to walk worthy of God (2:1–12); how they received the message as “the word of God” and suffered for it (2:13–16); and how he longed to see them (2:17–20). Chapter 3 tells of Timothy’s mission and ends in prayer that they will abound in love and be blameless (3:11–13). Chapters 4–5 supply what was lacking in their faith (3:10): holiness in the body (4:1–8), love and quiet work (4:9–12), the believers who have died (4:13–18), and the timing of the day of the Lord, which will come “like a thief in the night” (5:1–11). It closes with instructions for church life and a prayer that the God of peace will sanctify them completely (5:12–28). Every chapter reaches its close with the Lord’s coming in view (1:10; 2:19; 3:13; 4:16–17; 5:23).

Where it leads: to Christ. Within twenty years of the cross, Paul names “the Lord Jesus Christ” beside “God the Father” as the source of grace and peace (1:1), and prays to them together (3:11). “The day of the Lord”, which the prophets spoke of as the LORD’s own day of judgment, is now the day of Jesus’ coming. His death and resurrection ground all the letter’s hope: “since we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so, through Jesus, God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep” (4:14). He is the one who delivers us from the wrath to come (1:10), who “died for us so that whether we are awake or asleep we might live with him” (5:10). Paul’s picture of the Lord descending from heaven with a cry of command, an archangel’s voice and God’s trumpet (4:16–17) is one of the fullest in Scripture. This commentary reads it as the one visible return of Christ at the end of the age, when living believers are caught up to meet him and, like citizens going out to welcome a king, accompany him; dispensationalists read it as a secret rapture some years before his visible coming. Either way, the point is the last line: “so we will always be with the Lord.”

For us. This letter shows believers how to hold on in a hostile place: by trusting the word that converted them as God’s word, by expecting affliction (3:3–4), and by waiting for the Son from heaven. It gives Christians a way to grieve, not “as others do who have no hope” (4:13), but with tears that look towards a reunion. It asks them to work quietly, keep their bodies holy, love one another more and more, “Rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks in all circumstances” (5:16–18), and to stay awake. And it rests all of this not on their strength but on God: “He who calls you is faithful; he will surely do it” (5:24).

1.title: The Gospel That Works
1.overview:
Where we are. The opening of what is probably Paul’s earliest surviving letter. Chapters 1 to 3 look back over his short time with the Thessalonians; this thanksgiving sets the tone for all of it.

The message. The gospel works. When God sends his word with the power of the Holy Spirit, it makes people new, and the change can be seen: faith that works, love that toils, hope that endures. A church like that, however young and harassed, can be sure that God has chosen it and that its life is safe in the Father and the Son.

Why it was said. Paul had been driven out of the city after a few weeks, leaving behind a church of new converts under fierce pressure from their neighbours, and for months he could not bear the suspense (see the introduction). Timothy has just brought news that they are standing. Before answering critics or teaching what is lacking, Paul tells a frightened church what God has already done in it.

How the chapter makes its case. The greeting places this weeks-old assembly “in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ” (v. 1). Paul then thanks God for their faith, love and hope (vv. 2–3) and reasons from the fruit to the root: God has chosen them, as the way the gospel came to them proves, in power, in the Spirit and with full conviction, through men whose lives matched the message (vv. 4–5). Welcoming the word with joy under affliction, they became a pattern for the churches of Greece (vv. 6–7). Their story ran ahead of Paul everywhere (vv. 8–9), and its last line holds the whole Christian life: turned from idols, serving the living and true God, waiting for his Son (vv. 9–10).

Where it leads. The chapter ends with Jesus at both ends of the Christian life: already raised from the dead, and coming from heaven. Faith trusts him, love serves him, hope waits for him, and Paul gives him a present-tense name: Jesus who delivers us from the wrath to come. The waiting is not anxious, because the Rescuer is already at work.

For us. This chapter lets us test whether the gospel has done its work in us, not by a feeling but by its fruit. Ask what you have turned from, whom you now serve, and whether you are waiting for the Son. And if the fruit looks thin, look past it to the God who chose you in his love and the Son who rescues you still.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A weeks-old church in a hostile city is told where it really lives: in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. The three missionaries who founded it, Paul, Silas and Timothy, write together as friends (v. 1), and in one short sentence they set the Father and the Son side by side as the church’s home and the source of the grace and peace it needs.
verseByVerse.theology:
Paul says the church lives “in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ”. Naming the two together like this is a brief confession of who Christ is, and its date makes it striking (see the note on v. 1).

So even the greeting is praise to the Father and the Son together.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: In Thessalonica, kyrios (lord) was Caesar’s title. The charge laid against these believers was that they said there is another king, Jesus (Acts 17:7). A letter that calls Jesus “Lord” reminded them who really ruled over them and cared for them.

Now: Where he was loved and trusted, Paul used no title, only his name (on what that says to anyone who holds office, see the note on v. 1).

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy, To the church of the Thessalonians in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ: Grace to you and peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A young, persecuted church is greeted as people whose true home is God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, and who receive from him grace and peace. The setting is the relief of a man forced to leave this church after a few weeks, now writing from Corinth on hearing that it stands (3:1–6; see the introduction).

Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy. Silvanus is Silas of Acts, who sang hymns beside Paul in the Philippian stocks (Acts 16:24–25); Timothy will be sent back to Thessalonica alone, at some risk (3:2). Paul writes as one of a team.

In God the Father. Church (ekklēsia) was the ordinary Greek word for an assembly, above all the gathering of a city’s citizens to do the town’s business. Paul gives it to a scattering of former idol-worshippers, weeks old, in a town that had just run their teacher out, and tells them where they actually live. Thessalonica is only their address; they are the church “in God the Father”.

Grace to you and peace. The order never varies in Paul’s letters, because peace comes only from grace. Grace is God’s unearned favour; peace is what that favour brings: peace with God and then the settled wholeness of a life put right. Peace without grace is a truce that will not hold.

The Father and the Son under one “in”. One small word, “in”, covers both the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ: together they are the one in whom the church lives, and Paul offers no explanation. No Jew raised on the Shema, the confession that the LORD our God is one, does that casually. In one of the earliest Christian sentences we possess, about twenty years after the cross, Jesus already stands on the divine side of the line; the church did not slowly promote him over centuries.

What does it mean for a church to be in God? Its existence and security rest in him, not in its numbers, building, reputation or leaders: held by the Father’s care and joined to Christ as a body to its head, its life cannot be ended by those who oppose it. That frees a small or struggling congregation from measuring itself by what the town thinks. The Thessalonians had no building, no history and no apostle, and they were still an assembly whose true location is the Father and the Son. Your church, however ordinary its Sunday looks, is that too.

Why does Paul leave out his apostleship here? Because nothing in Thessalonica required him to defend it, so he wrote as a friend alongside his fellow workers. A quiet lesson for anyone with a title: use it when the truth needs defending, and set it aside when love can do the work. Authority in the church is a trust for others’ good, not a badge to wear.

Textual note. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, add “from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ” after “peace”; the earliest do not, so most modern Bibles have the shorter greeting.
verseByVerse.note: Thessalonica was the capital of Macedonia and a busy port on the Via Egnatia, Rome’s great east–west road. Paul founded the church on his second journey but was soon driven out. Silvanus is the Silas of Acts. Paul probably wrote from Corinth around AD 50, making this one of his earliest letters.

verseByVerse.ref: 1:2–10 – Faith, Love, Hope — and a Church Everyone Was Talking About
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The gospel had plainly done its work in Thessalonica, and Paul thanks God for it. He remembers their faith, love and hope, each seen in what it produces (vv. 2–3), and is sure God has chosen them, because the message came with the Spirit’s power and they welcomed it with joy under persecution (vv. 4–7). The news of their conversion spread so far that Paul had nothing to add (vv. 8–9), and its last line sums up the whole Christian life: turned from idols, serving the living God, waiting for his Son (vv. 9–10).
verseByVerse.theology:
Election, and how anyone could know

Paul reasons back from the result to its cause: the gospel arrived with power, the Spirit and settled conviction, and it produced work, labour and endurance; therefore God had chosen them (on how Paul could know, see the notes on vv. 4–5). God did not choose them because of their faith and love; the reason lies wholly in him. But their faith and love are the evidence that he chose them.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul had perhaps a month in the city (Acts 17:2), yet this church became the pattern held up to others (see the note on vv. 6–7).

Now: What travelled was the report of changed, glad people (see the note on v. 8).

verseByVerse.quote: We give thanks to God always for all of you, constantly mentioning you in our prayers,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s first word to a frightened church is thanks to God for every one of them, offered constantly in prayer. Before he answers any slander or corrects anything, he tells them what God has already done in them.

Always, all, constantly. Paul had left this church in the worst circumstances and spent months unable to bear the suspense (3:5); yet thanksgiving was his settled response. “Constantly” means unceasingly (also 2:13; 5:17): a habit, not a mood; this church came up every time he prayed. Verses 2 to 5 are one long sentence in Greek, and the thanks spills over again later (2:13; 3:9). It goes to God, not to the Thessalonians, because their faith is his work: he makes faith where there was none, and keeps it alive in a hostile city when the apostle has been driven away.

A greater intercessor. Behind Paul’s prayers stands an intercession that never breaks. Before the cross, the Lord Jesus prayed not only for his apostles but for those who would believe in him through their word (John 17:20), a company of former idol-worshippers in a Macedonian port among them, and he always lives to intercede for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25; Romans 8:34). That is the deepest reason Paul can give thanks for a church he cannot reach: its life never hung on the apostle, but on the Son at the Father’s right hand.

What Paul did with his worry. Worried sick and unable to reach them, Paul turns the worry into thanks and intercession without waiting for good news. Do the same with anxiety about people you love: carry it to God, and begin with what he has already done in them.

How can I pray for people constantly when the list keeps growing? Pray regularly rather than exhaustively. Many Christians keep a short list for each day of the week, so that everyone comes round in turn, and pray in a sentence as people come to mind, at the sink or on the bus. Begin, as Paul does, with thanks for what God has done in them, then ask for what they need. You will not pray for everyone every day, and you need not; what matters is that the people God has given you are not forgotten before him.

Why thank God, and not the person? Because faith, love and hope are gifts before they are achievements. Encouraging people is right, and Paul does it warmly in this very letter; but thanking God for a brother’s faith tells the truth about where it came from, and keeps you both from pride.

verseByVerse.quote: remembering before our God and Father your work of faith and labor of love and steadfastness of hope in our Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul remembers before God the faith, love and hope that Christ has produced in them, each one visible in what it does: faith works, love toils, hope endures. This may be the earliest appearance in writing of the famous triad.

Your work of faith. Faith produces work: not work that earns anything, but work that faith itself generates, as a live root pushes up a shoot (Galatians 5:6; James 2:18). A faith that has changed nothing about what you do is a faith Paul would not recognise.

And labour of love. Love produces labour (kopos): toil to the point of weariness, the tiredness of doing something hard for somebody else. Most real love in a church looks like being worn out by people: the meals cooked, the hospital visits, the long conversation with someone who keeps returning to the same grief.

And steadfastness of hope. Hope produces steadfastness (hypomonē): the staying power of someone who keeps going under a weight without buckling. You can bear almost anything if you know it ends, and how, and these persecuted believers were fed by what was coming: the return of Christ.

In our Lord Jesus Christ. Not admirable human qualities but what Christ produces in people joined to him, as a vine’s life flows into its branches (John 15:5). Faith looks back to what he has done, love looks around to others for his sake, and hope looks forward to his coming: he is the one faith trusts, love serves and hope waits for. He makes weak people work, tired people love, and frightened people stand, and when the work is done, the labour spent and the waiting over, he himself will be the reward. Paul returns to the three again and again (5:8; 1 Corinthians 13:13).

A test from the verse. Ask not whether you have faith, love and hope, but whether anything in your week would be different if you did not. If that question troubles you, the trouble is itself a sign of life: dead faith does not worry about its fruit. None of us bears this fruit perfectly; Christ alone obeyed perfectly, in our place, and for his sake God accepts our flawed work. Bring the weak fruit to him; the Holy Spirit, now living in you, is the one who grows it.

Is the work of faith the same as the works Paul rejects in Galatians? No. The works Paul rejects are works done to earn a right standing with God, as though our obedience could pay for acceptance. The work of faith is what faith does after God has freely accepted us in Christ: it trusts him, and so it obeys, serves, forgives and keeps going. The first is a wage; the second is a fruit. A Christian works hard, but from acceptance, not for it.

What if my love feels more like exhaustion than affection? Then you may be closer to this verse than you think: Paul chose the word for weary toil, and being tired from loving people is often a sign that love is real. But exhaustion needs care: rest, prayer, and other believers sharing the load. Love that labours must keep drawing from Christ, or it will curdle into resentment. Ask him for strength, and ask the church for help.
verseByVerse.note: Faith, love and hope — the triad Paul returns to again and again.

verseByVerse.quote: For we know, brothers loved by God, that he has chosen you,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul is sure that God, out of his love, has chosen these believers, and he tells them so to steady them. Their standing rests not on their own grip on God but on his choice of them.

Brothers loved by God. The Greek form (ēgapēmenoi) describes a love that began in the past and still stands: a settled state, not a mood God is in on a good day. This love, not anything in them, is the reason he chose them (Deuteronomy 7:7–8; Ephesians 1:4–5). And “brothers”, used of the whole church, men and women together, tells people who had lost their families by turning from the gods that they have a new one.

That he has chosen you. Election (eklogē) is God’s choosing of some for salvation in Christ before the world began, for reasons in his love and not in us (2 Thessalonians 2:13). See where Paul puts this doctrine some find cold: in a letter to frightened, persecuted people, as the first solid ground he can give them. If their standing rested on their own decision, a bad enough month could undo it. If it rests on his choice, it cannot.

How could Paul know? This is the question people ask in the car park afterwards. No one on earth has seen the list of names, and Paul claims no private revelation. He gives his evidence in the next word, “because” (v. 5): he knows they were chosen from how the gospel arrived among them and what it did. God’s choice is hidden, like a root; its fruit can be seen (2 Peter 1:10). So Paul does not use election as a threat or to sort the congregation, but the way you would hand a deed of title to a nervous tenant: this is yours, and here is why nobody can take it.

Chosen in the Beloved. God chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world, and blessed us in the Beloved (Ephesians 1:4–6). Election is inclusion in the Father’s love for his beloved Son (Matthew 3:17): not freestanding individuals whose record God keeps checking, but people joined to the Son. On a bad day, God’s love for you is as steady as his love for Jesus, because it is the same love (John 17:23).

Not one link was forged by them. Before the world was made, God set his love on people who would one day bow to idols in a Greek port, and did not change his mind when they did. He sent his Son to die for them, a tired missionary to tell them, and the Spirit to open their ears. Not one link in that chain was forged by them, and not one can be broken by them.

I cannot see much fruit in my life. Does that mean I am not chosen? Look at the right things. The fruit is not spiritual brilliance but the marks Paul lists: you believe the gospel is true; you have turned, however falteringly, from what you once served; you love God’s people; you keep coming back to Christ when you fail. Weak faith in Christ is still faith in Christ. And assurance is not first found by staring inward but by looking to Christ, who casts out none who come to him (John 6:37). Whoever comes is chosen; election is God’s explanation of why you came.

If God has chosen, why should I pray for unbelievers or share the gospel? Because God saves his people through prayer and preaching, and gives us the privilege of being his means. Election makes evangelism hopeful, not pointless. In Corinth, when Paul was opposed, the Lord told him that he had many people in that city (Acts 18:10), and the promise kept him preaching there for eighteen months. We do not know who the elect are, so we tell everyone, and pray expecting God to open hearts.

Where Christians differ: can we know who is elect? Some say election is unknowable and therefore irrelevant; others claim to know others’ eternal destiny. Some Christians (Arminians) hold, out of sincere concern for God’s fairness, that God chose those he foresaw would believe; many are devoted servants of Christ. But Paul knows they were chosen because the gospel came to them in power and in the Holy Spirit (v. 5) and they received it: their faith is the evidence of God’s choice, not its cause. This commentary’s view: Election is God’s free choice before the foundation of the world, not based on foreseen faith (Ephesians 1:4; Romans 9:11). We cannot read God’s secret will directly, but election shows itself in its fruits: the gospel received with power and conviction, a turning from idols, faith, love and hope (vv. 3–10; 2 Peter 1:10). So believers may have assurance of their election, and the church may speak of believers as chosen, while leaving final judgment to God, as the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession both teach (Westminster 3.8; 1689 3.7).

verseByVerse.quote: because our gospel came to you not only in word, but also in power and in the Holy Spirit and with full conviction. You know what kind of men we proved to be among you for your sake.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul knows they were chosen because the gospel reached them as more than words: the Holy Spirit made it powerful and convincing, and the preachers’ lives backed it up. The same message can leave one room unmoved and another changed for ever, and the difference is not the sermon.

Not only in word. The gospel did come in word: it was preached, it had content, it was argued from the Scriptures for three Sabbaths, and there is no gospel without words.

In power and in the Holy Spirit. Words are the tool, but the Spirit is the one who works: he made the words effective and changed hearts (Romans 1:16; 1 Corinthians 2:4). The gospel’s outward call goes to everyone who hears it, but the Spirit’s inward call opens the heart, so that the hearer actually comes, as the Lord opened Lydia’s heart in Philippi a few weeks earlier (Acts 16:14).

What kind of men we proved to be. Paul points to the messengers themselves: men who arrived with their backs still marked from a flogging in Philippi (2:2), and who worked night and day at a trade so as not to burden anybody (2:9). The Spirit gives the power; a life gives the credibility.

This Jesus is the Christ. Luke tells us what Paul argued in that synagogue: that “it was necessary for the Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead”, and that this Jesus, whom he proclaimed, is the Christ (Acts 17:3). The power came with a message about a crucified man, because the Spirit’s work is to glorify Christ, taking what is his and making it known (John 16:14); and men with flogged backs, preaching a Messiah who suffered before he reigned, were living illustrations of it.

Loving a man they had never seen. Praise to the Holy Spirit, who takes ordinary words from ordinary mouths and makes them the voice of God to a dead heart. He did it in a Thessalonian synagogue with an argument about a cross, and the hearers found themselves loving a man they had never seen (1 Peter 1:8). No preacher can make anyone love Christ; every believer alive is proof of the Spirit’s work.

Does power mean miracles? Should we expect them when we preach? Paul may include the signs that accompanied the apostles’ ministry (Romans 15:19), but his main point is the power that converts: the Spirit opening blind eyes to the truth of Christ. This commentary’s view is cessationist (the view that the miraculous sign-gifts ceased with the apostles), held charitably: the sign-gifts that authenticated the apostles and their message belonged to that founding period, while the Spirit’s converting power goes on in every age, because Scripture itself calls those signs the marks of an apostle and ties them to the first witnesses (2 Corinthians 12:12; Hebrews 2:3–4). Many faithful Christians, Pentecostal and charismatic, believe the gifts continue, and this commentary honours them as brothers and sisters. So yes, expect power when the gospel is preached, the greatest power there is: dead hearts made alive. That is a greater wonder than a healed body, and God still does it.

Was this full conviction just the excitement of a crowd? A fair question: crowds can be stirred to believe anything for an evening. But this conviction did not fade when the preachers left town by night; it held through months of hostility from neighbours and families (2:14), with no apostle to keep it warm. Crowd excitement needs the crowd. This needed nothing but the word and the Spirit, and it made people steady rather than giddy: the mark of God’s hand, not of a good meeting.

I have never preached a sermon. Does this verse apply to me? Yes. Every Christian who speaks of Christ to a friend, a child or a colleague does on a smaller scale what Paul did: speaks true words, depending on the Spirit to make them live, from a life that does not contradict them. You cannot supply the power and are not asked to; you are asked to say what is true, kindly and clearly, and to live so that your words are believable.

Uncertain wording. “Full conviction” translates plērophoria (with “much”), a rare word that can mean full assurance or simply fullness. It is also unclear whose conviction is meant: the preachers’, who spoke with settled, unhesitating certainty, or the hearers’, who were fully persuaded. The ESV’s “full conviction” is the likely sense, and probably it was true on both sides.

verseByVerse.quote: And you became imitators of us and of the Lord, for you received the word in much affliction, with the joy of the Holy Spirit, so that you became an example to all the believers in Macedonia and in Achaia.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Thessalonians welcomed the gospel with Spirit-given joy in the middle of persecution, copying their teachers and their Lord, and so became a pattern for the believers of all Greece.

Imitators of us and of the Lord. They copied not Paul’s gifts but the way he took a beating and kept his joy. They had watched him preach with his back marked from Philippi, and when the same trouble came on them, they behaved the same way. Imitation in the New Testament is rarely copying a technique; it is having watched somebody under pressure and finding, when your turn comes, that you do what they did.

In much affliction. Affliction (thlipsis) is crushing pressure: riots, and their own countrymen turned against them (Acts 17:5–9; 2:14).

With the joy of the Holy Spirit. Not joy they worked up, but something the Spirit produced while the pressure was still on (Acts 13:52). Joy inside affliction is a fact that demands an explanation, and people go looking for one.

An example. An example (typos) is the impression a stamp leaves: the gospel had left its mark on them, and other churches could read it off them. Macedonia and Achaia were the northern and southern provinces of Greece. Paul had been with them a matter of weeks, and already these new converts are the pattern held up to two Roman provinces. How long you have been a Christian does not decide how useful you are to God.

And of the Lord. Behind Paul stands the Lord himself, who “for the joy that was set before him endured the cross” (Hebrews 12:2). Joy and suffering were held together first in him.

Is it wrong to feel sad or afraid when I suffer? No. The Lord Jesus wept and was troubled in spirit, and Paul writes of grief and anxiety in this letter (2:17; 3:5). The Spirit’s joy is not a fixed smile or a denial of pain but a deeper gladness that Christ is yours and nothing can take him from you, a joy that can sit beside sorrow and outlast it. If you cannot feel it today, ask for it; it is his gift, not your achievement.

Is it right to imitate human leaders? Yes, so far as they imitate Christ (1 Corinthians 11:1). God gives his church living examples because we learn best by watching. But we copy the man only in order to follow the Lord: copy a Christian’s faith, patience and love; never make him your master, and never follow him where he departs from Christ.
verseByVerse.note: Achaia was the Roman province of southern Greece, with Corinth as its capital.

verseByVerse.quote: For not only has the word of the Lord sounded forth from you in Macedonia and Achaia, but your faith in God has gone forth everywhere, so that we need not say anything.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The news of their faith spread so far and so fast that Paul found he had nothing to add.

Sounded forth. A word for a sound that rings out and carries, like a trumpet or rolling thunder (exēcheō, from which we get echo). The gospel struck this church like a hammer on a bell, and the ringing went out across the province. The Greek tense means it sounded and is still sounding: it has reached you.

Gone forth everywhere. Travellers, traders and sailors carried the story along the Via Egnatia (see Roads and Travel). “Everywhere” is the natural overstatement of a delighted man.

We need not say anything. Paul arrives somewhere to talk about the gospel, finds people telling him about the Thessalonians first, and is delighted not to be needed. What travelled was not a programme but a report: people in Thessalonica had dropped their idols and would not stop being glad about it under pressure. A church that chases a good name soon shapes its message to please the audience; a good name that follows from changed lives points away from the church to the Lord who changed them.

The word of the Lord. The Lord here is most likely the Lord Jesus, as usually in Paul, and the word is his. He had told his apostles they would be his witnesses to the end of the earth (Acts 1:8). What rang out from Thessalonica was the risen Christ keeping his promise.

Does every Christian have to evangelise? I am shy and not good with words. Every Christian is a witness, but not every Christian is a preacher. The Thessalonians spread the word first by being a visible, changed people, and then by speaking when asked (1 Peter 3:15). You can do both. Live openly as a Christian, let people know you go to church and why, pray for those around you, invite them to hear the gospel, and when someone asks why you have hope, tell them simply what Christ has done for you. The Lord uses quiet voices; he asks faithfulness, not eloquence.

Is the word of the Lord the Bible, or the spoken gospel? Here it is the gospel about Christ, spoken and passed on: not new revelation from the church but the apostolic gospel it had received, repeated faithfully. That same word God has now given us, fixed and complete, in Scripture.

verseByVerse.quote: For they themselves report concerning us the kind of reception we had among you, and how you turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God,
verseByVerse.commentary:
People everywhere were telling how the missionaries had come and how the Thessalonians had turned from their idols to serve the living and true God. Verses 9 and 10 are among the shortest summaries of conversion in the New Testament.

The kind of reception we had among you. The report begins with the missionaries themselves (see the uncertain wording below). Paul picks up the same word in 2:1 (“our coming to you”), where he begins to answer those who were slandering the way he had come and gone.

Turned to God from idols. To God first, and so away from idols. That is nearly always how it happens: people rarely put down an idol because they have been persuaded it is worthless, but because something better has taken hold of them. And “from idols” tells us most of this church were converted pagans.

What it cost in that city. Thessalonica was thick with the worship of Dionysus, Serapis and, most dangerously, the emperor; the trade guilds had patron gods and sacrificial meals, and family life ran on household deities. To turn from idols was to resign from the life of the town, which goes a long way to explain the affliction of verse 6.

To serve the living and true God. Both words are aimed at idols. An idol is not living: Isaiah mocked the man who burns half a tree to warm himself and worships the other half (Isaiah 44:14–17); and it is not true, for there is no real god behind it. Paul uses Jeremiah’s language for the LORD, the true God and the living God (Jeremiah 10:10). To serve here is to serve as a slave (douleuō), and the blunt word is deliberate. They did not exchange slavery for independence; they changed masters. The question is never whether to serve but which master is worth it, and only one died for his servants.

Him who is true. John closes his first letter with the same pair, the true God and idols, and shows where the true God is known: the Son of God has come and given us understanding, so that we may know him who is true, and we are in him who is true, in his Son Jesus Christ (1 John 5:20–21). People make idols in their own image; the living God made himself known by becoming man.

The only freedom there is. The idols of Thessalonica are dust. He is living, and he gives life; he is true, and he never deceives. The gods of the city had to be fed; this God came looking for people who had bowed to wood and stone, opened his house to them, and set them at his table as sons. Glory to the living and true God, whose service is the only freedom there is.

How do I find my idols if I own no statues? Modern people have idols too: anything we trust, love or fear more than God is one (Colossians 3:5), shrine or no shrine. Ask what you serve: what you organise your week around, what you are afraid of losing, what you daydream about, what you would sacrifice sleep, money and integrity to keep, and what makes you angry or despairing when it is threatened. Good things become idols when we ask them to give what only God can give: security, worth, comfort, control.

How do I actually turn from an idol? The way the Thessalonians did: by turning to God first. Confess it to him by name. Look hard at the living and true God, his goodness, his promises, his Son, until the idol looks small beside him. Cut off what feeds it where you can, and replace it with service: give away some of the money, use the time for others, bring the fear to God every time it rises. Expect to turn again and again. Old idols rarely leave in one day, but a heart that has seen the living God never fully goes back.

Uncertain wording. “The kind of reception we had” is one Greek word, eisodos, normally an entering or visit. It can describe how the missionaries came among them (its sense in 2:1) or how they were received. Probably both are in view: people talked about how Paul came as well as the welcome he was given.
verseByVerse.note: Turning “from idols” shows that most of the church were converted pagans, not Jews.

verseByVerse.quote: and to wait for his Son from heaven, whom he raised from the dead, Jesus who delivers us from the wrath to come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christians live waiting for God’s Son to come from heaven: the Jesus he raised from the dead, who even now rescues them from the judgment to come.

To wait for his Son. The waiting (anamenō) is not idleness but expectancy, like watching a road for someone you love. Within weeks of conversion these believers had their eyes on the horizon, and the second coming runs through every chapter of this letter (2:19; 3:13; 4:13–18; 5:1–11, 23).

Whom he raised from the dead. The return rests on something that has already happened in public: the resurrection proves he is God’s Son and guarantees his return as Judge (Acts 17:31; Romans 1:4). A man who has been raised is a man who can come back.

The wrath to come. Not divine temper, but God’s settled, just opposition to evil (see the question below): his judgment on sin at the end (Romans 2:5; 5:9), when the accounts of history will finally be settled.

The tense is the comfort. Paul does not tell frightened, persecuted people that wrath is coming for them. Jesus delivers (rhyomai, rescues), and the Greek form is present: literally, Jesus the one rescuing us, almost a title: Jesus our Rescuer. The wrath is future; the deliverance is a fact now, secured by the one who bore on the cross the judgment his people deserved. So we wait for him, not as criminals for a judge but as a bride for her husband.

A whole life in ten verses. They turned in the past, they serve now, and they wait for what is coming; and Jesus stands at both ends, already raised and soon to come.

Why would a loving God have wrath at all? Because love that does not oppose evil is not love: a father who felt nothing when his child was abused would not be loving but indifferent. God’s wrath is the resistance of his holiness and love to everything that destroys what he made. The wonder of the gospel is not that God has no wrath, but that he himself, in his Son, bore it for us, so that his justice and his mercy meet at the cross (Romans 3:25–26).

I still sin. Am I really safe from the wrath to come? Yes, if you are in Christ. Your rescue rests not on how well you have done this week but on what Jesus did once for all and is doing for you now. The wrath your sins deserve fell on him; there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). Your continuing sin should grieve you and drive you back to him, but it cannot reopen a case he has closed.

Does waiting for Jesus mean I should try to work out when he will come? No. No one knows the day or hour (Matthew 24:36); the day comes like a thief (5:2). Waiting means living ready, not calculating dates: holding this world loosely, serving faithfully where you are, and being glad, not afraid, at the thought of his coming, which is always near (Philippians 4:5).

Where Christians differ: wrath and the rapture. Some read deliverance from the wrath to come (here and 5:9) as a promise that believers will be removed from the earth in a secret rapture (from the Latin for being caught up, 4:17) before a seven-year tribulation. Many earnest, Bible-loving Christians hold this, reasoning that the tribulation is God’s wrath and his people are not destined for it. This commentary’s view: The wrath to come is God’s final judgment on the ungodly at the last day (Romans 2:5; 2 Thessalonians 1:7–9). Believers are rescued from it through Christ’s death and resurrection. This does not promise escape from all suffering beforehand; the Thessalonians were already suffering (v. 6; 3:3). Christ will return once, visibly, to raise the dead, rescue his people and judge the world. There is no secret rapture. The reason: Paul describes one public coming, with a shout and a trumpet (4:16), and when he speaks of our being gathered to Christ he says that day will not come until the rebellion and the man of lawlessness appear first (2 Thessalonians 2:1–3).
