You know what kind of men we proved to be among you for your sake.<sup>6</sup>And you became imitators of us and of the Lord, for you received the word in much affliction, with the joy of the Holy Spirit,<sup>7</sup>so that you became an example to all the believers in Macedonia and in Achaia.<sup>8</sup>For not only has the word of the Lord sounded forth from you in Macedonia and Achaia, but your faith in God has gone forth everywhere, so that we need not say anything.<sup>9</sup>For they themselves report concerning us the kind of reception we had among you, and how you turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God,<sup>10</sup>and to wait for his Son from heaven, whom he raised from the dead, Jesus who delivers us from the wrath to come.

keyVerse.quote: you turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God, and to wait for his Son from heaven, whom he raised from the dead, Jesus who delivers us from the wrath to come.
keyVerse.note: These words, which other people were repeating about the Thessalonians, hold the whole Christian life in three verbs: turned, serve, wait. They show the proof of God’s choosing that Paul has been describing, and they end where the whole letter ends, with the risen Jesus coming from heaven as his people’s Rescuer.

1.reflection:
Paul measures faith, love and hope by what they produce: work, labour and steadfastness (v. 3). If someone looked only at your last month, which of the three would they see most clearly, and which least?

Paul is sure the Thessalonians were chosen because of how the gospel came to them and what it did (vv. 4–5). How does this help a believer who doubts, and how does it guard against both pride and presumption?

The Thessalonians received the word “in much affliction, with the joy of the Holy Spirit” (v. 6). Have you seen joy and suffering held together in someone’s life? What made it possible?

Turning to God “from idols” cost these believers their place in the life of the city (v. 9). What are the idols of our culture, and what would it cost you to turn from them to serve the living and true God?

2.title: A Nursing Mother and a Urging Father
2.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 1 thanked God for how the gospel came to Thessalonica and what it did there. Chapter 2 looks at the same events from the other side: how the messengers lived among them, how the church received the message, and why Paul has not come back.

The message. The gospel they believed was God’s own word, carried by men who were trustworthy because they wanted nothing from them except their good. He had loved them like a mother and trained them like a father, and he had not abandoned them. The word is now at work in them, and their suffering for it puts them in good company.

Why it was said. After Paul’s hurried departure by night, someone was evidently calling him just another travelling religious salesman who flattered people for money and ran when it got hard (see the introduction). If the messenger was a fraud, the message might be too, and a frightened young church under persecution could easily be talked out of its faith.

How the chapter makes its case. Paul appeals to what they saw with their own eyes (vv. 1–12): his arrival bruised from Philippi, preaching with God-given boldness; a message entrusted by God, without flattery, greed or a claim to status; a nursing mother’s gentleness; nights at a workbench so that the gospel could be free; a father’s urging to walk worthy of God. He thanks God that they received the message as God’s word, which proved itself by holding them firm under persecution, as it had the churches in Judea (vv. 13–16). Then his grief shows (vv. 17–20): “torn away” from them, blocked by Satan, he still counts them his hope, joy and crown when the Lord Jesus comes.

Where it leads. Behind this portrait of a true pastor stands, at every turn, the Shepherd whose likeness Paul bears: the Son who always pleased his Father, who though he was in the form of God did not insist on his rights, who gave not only his time but himself, and who was shamefully treated before his servants were. And the chapter ends with that Lord coming as King, his people going out to meet him.

For us. This chapter shows what to look for in those who teach us and what to be for those we serve: true words, pure motives, gentleness, hard work and a love that gives itself. It asks whether we receive the Bible as God’s word that judges us, and it tells us that our hope on the last day is not what we achieved but the people we loved for Christ’s sake.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A true minister of the gospel is known by his life, and Paul’s life among them had been open to inspection. He came in courage straight from a beating at Philippi, and his coming bore fruit (vv. 1–2). His message came from God, not from error, impure motives or trickery, because he works to please the God who tests hearts (vv. 3–4), so he used no flattery, no cover for greed and no claim to status (vv. 5–6). Instead he was gentle as a nursing mother and shared his very life (vv. 7–8), worked night and day to preach free of charge (v. 9), and like a father urged each one to walk worthy of the God who calls them into his kingdom and glory (vv. 10–12).
verseByVerse.theology:
The minister as steward, not owner

The governing idea of the passage is in verse 4: entrusted with the gospel. A minister stands under the word, not over it, and works for God’s approval, not people’s (see the note on vv. 3–4).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The cities Paul visited were full of travelling lecturers who made their living by fine speaking. So Paul answers with what could be checked (see vv. 1–2 and v. 9).

Now: For anyone holding office, the question is what you intend to do with your rights (see the note on vv. 5–6).

verseByVerse.quote: For you yourselves know, brothers, that our coming to you was not in vain. But though we had already suffered and been shamefully treated at Philippi, as you know, we had boldness in our God to declare to you the gospel of God in the midst of much conflict.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s visit to them was not empty: fresh from a beating at Philippi, he preached in Thessalonica with a courage that God gave him. They know this themselves.

The accusation behind the chapter. You can tell what it was from what Paul denies: that he was a flatterer, after money, chasing a reputation, and that he ran when it got difficult. Travelling philosophers and religious salesmen worked those roads constantly, and the easiest way to damage a young church was to persuade it that its founder had been one more of them. So Paul keeps saying “you know”: his defence is their own memory.

Not in vain. In vain means empty, hollow (kenos). The congregation reading the letter was the proof that his visit was not.

Shamefully treated at Philippi. There he and Silas had been stripped in the marketplace, beaten with rods and fastened in the stocks (Acts 16:22–24), illegally, since they were Roman citizens. He arrived in Thessalonica, a hundred miles on, still marked.

Boldness in our God. He preached anyway. The verb (parrēsiazomai) is the freedom to speak openly, and its source is “in our God”, not his own nerve: courage God gave him, the opposite of the self-promotion he was accused of. God brought him from the stocks of Philippi to the synagogue of Thessalonica and opened his mouth there.

In the midst of much conflict. Conflict (agōn) is the struggle in the arena, and it ended in a riot (Acts 17:5). Here is the chapter’s argument in one sentence: a man in it for money or applause does not walk from a flogging in one city into a riot in the next.

Shamefully treated, like his Lord. Paul’s word for Philippi (hybrizō) is the word Jesus used of his own coming suffering: the Son of Man would be delivered over to the Gentiles and mocked and shamefully treated and spat upon (Luke 18:32). Paul was walking where his Lord had walked first (Acts 5:41). A man who preaches a Christ who was insulted and beaten does not find insult a reason to stop; he finds it a strange confirmation that he belongs to the one he preaches.

Where does boldness come from, if I am naturally timid? From God, not from temperament. Paul did not say he was brave; he said he had boldness in our God. Such courage grows from being sure of the message, sure of the God who sends it, and more concerned for the hearer than for yourself. Pray for it, as the apostles did (Acts 4:29), then take the next small step: one honest sentence about Christ to one person. Boldness is usually given in the act of obeying, not beforehand.

Should I keep speaking about Christ after I have been hurt for it? Usually yes, though wisdom matters. Paul left Philippi, as he left more than one hostile place, but did not go silent; he preached in the next city. Being hurt is not a sign God has withdrawn his call. Bring the wound to him, let others in the church care for you, and speak again when he opens the door.
verseByVerse.note: At Philippi Paul and Silas had been beaten and jailed just before they came to Thessalonica.

verseByVerse.quote: For our appeal does not spring from error or impurity or any attempt to deceive, but just as we have been approved by God to be entrusted with the gospel, so we speak, not to please man, but to please God who tests our hearts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s preaching came from God, not from error, impure motives or trickery, because he speaks as a man trusted with someone else’s message and answerable to the God who sees the heart.

Error, impurity, deceit. Three ways a ministry goes wrong. Error (planē) is in the message: a man may be sincere and simply wrong. Impurity (akatharsia) is in the motive, and the word often carried a sexual edge; a travelling teacher with access to households was a known hazard. Deceit (dolos) is in the method: the angler’s art of hiding the hook. Any one of them ruins a ministry that is sound in the other two.

Approved by God. The metalworker’s word (dokimazō) for testing metal and finding it genuine. Paul did not appoint himself: God tested him, found him fit and gave him the gospel to carry (1 Timothy 1:12), and goes on examining his heart every time he speaks.

Entrusted. Like a steward with his master’s goods (1 Corinthians 4:1–2), Paul is a courier carrying something that belongs to someone else, and a courier does not get to edit the parcel.

To please God who tests our hearts. Everything turns on this (Galatians 1:10). Paul is not indifferent to people, as the tenderness that follows shows; the question is whose approval he works for. People and God often want different things: people can be pleased by softening what is hard, and God sees the heart while you do it.

The one who always pleased the Father. Jesus said of the Father, “I always do the things that are pleasing to him” (John 8:29), and yet “Christ did not please himself” (Romans 15:3): he slipped away from the crowd that wanted to make him king by force (John 6:15), and refused the devil’s offer of the kingdoms without a cross (Matthew 4:8–10). Every faithful courier of the gospel copies that one life, and falls short of it.

A heart that passed every test. The gospel is God’s treasure, not ours, and he has been pleased to put it into clay jars, carrying a light that is not their own (2 Corinthians 4:7). The God who tests hearts found in his Son a heart that passed every test, and he has made that Son our righteousness, so that tried and failing servants stand approved in him.

What does it look like to please people rather than God? Leaving out the parts of the truth that would cost you: never mentioning repentance or judgment, agreeing with whoever is in the room, staying silent when a friend is going wrong. It is often fear dressed up as kindness. Pleasing God does not mean being harsh; Paul was gentle. It means saying the true thing in a loving way, and letting God judge the result.

verseByVerse.quote: For we never came with words of flattery, as you know, nor with a pretext for greed—God is witness. Nor did we seek glory from people, whether from you or from others, though we could have made demands as apostles of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul never used the gospel to get anything for himself: not favour by flattery, not money, not admiration, not even the support he had a right to as an apostle.

Words of flattery. Saying what a person wants to hear in order to get something from them: praise with a hook in it. Here Paul appeals to their memory: you heard what I said.

A pretext for greed. A pretext (prophasis) is a cover story: ministry as a front for making money. But greed is a motive, and motives are invisible, so Paul calls the one witness who can see them.

Glory from people. Subtler than money and more common among religious people: a man can be scrupulous about cash and still feed on being admired. And “whether from you or from others” means he was not building a reputation to spend somewhere else.

We could have made demands. As apostles they could have insisted on their position and asked to be supported (see below). Paul defends that right elsewhere (1 Corinthians 9:4–14), and here declines to press it.

When friendship becomes a sales channel. Paul’s cities were full of travelling speakers who lived on fees and admiration, and writers of his century, such as the orator Dio Chrysostom, complained of men who flattered the crowd and called it philosophy. We have our own version, in which warmth is a marketing strategy and the friend on a screen is building an audience to sell to. The result is a quiet cynicism: everyone, we suspect, is after something. The suspicion is not foolish, and the church has given it plenty of material. But it leaves us lonely, because if every kindness is a pitch, nobody can ever simply be loved.

The mind of Christ. Paul’s answer is not a cleverer technique but a man who worked night and day so as not to be a weight on anyone (v. 9), and behind him a Lord who needed nothing from us and gave himself anyway, who, though he was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped (Philippians 2:6). The Son of God had every right in heaven and on earth, and did not insist on one of them. Only someone who already has everything in Christ can afford to love people without using them. In ministry, as wherever one person holds power, the question is rarely whether you have a right, but what you intend to do with it.

How can I tell encouragement from flattery in myself? Ask three questions. Is it true? Flattery exaggerates or invents. Is it for their good or for mine? Flattery wants something back. Would I say it behind their back too? Flattery is spoken to the face only. Encouragement names real grace in someone, specifically, and gives God the credit. Practise it freely; the church is starved of it.

Is it wrong to want to be appreciated? No. Paul longed to be loved by his churches. What is wrong is making praise the reason you serve, so that you sulk when it is missing or shape the work to get it. Do the work for God, receive thanks gratefully, and pass the glory on.

Uncertain wording. “We could have made demands” is literally we could have been in weight (en barei). That can mean being a financial weight, living at the church’s expense (the same root comes in v. 9, “not be a burden”), or carrying weight, standing on their dignity as apostles. The context of greed and glory suits both, and Paul may intend both: he claimed neither their money nor their deference.

verseByVerse.quote: But we were gentle among you, like a nursing mother taking care of her own children. So, being affectionately desirous of you, we were ready to share with you not only the gospel of God but also our own selves, because you had become very dear to us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Instead of using them, Paul cared for them as tenderly as a mother nursing her own baby, and gave them his very life along with the gospel, because he had come to love them.

But we were gentle among you. Having said what he was not, Paul says what he was. Gentle (ēpioi) is the opposite of domineering: Paul, so stern in Galatians, is soft with these new believers.

Like a nursing mother. The words “her own” matter: not a hired wet nurse minding somebody else’s baby, but a mother feeding her own child. The verb (thalpō) means to cherish, to keep warm, and is used of a bird brooding over her eggs: the most ordinary and costly self-giving, at night, unseen.

Affectionately desirous. The ache of wanting someone you cannot reach (see below): that is what Paul felt for a church he had known for a month or so.

Our own selves. Selves (psychai) means lives: time, energy, hearts. You can deliver the message accurately and keep yourself back, and much professional religion is exactly that: correct teaching from a careful distance.

Very dear to us. That is the reason, and it is not a strategy. Love hands over more than was required, and anyone served by someone who plainly liked them knows the difference.

More than his life shared. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11), the same word for life that Paul uses here. But Paul offered his time, strength and heart; Christ “loved me and gave himself for me” (Galatians 2:20), and at his table says, this is my body, given for you (Luke 22:19; 1 Corinthians 11:24). Paul gave himself along with his message; Christ himself is the message, and he gave himself completely.

The God who would not forget. Before Paul was a nursing mother to Thessalonica, God was one to Israel: can a woman forget her nursing child? Even these may forget, yet I will not forget you, says the LORD (Isaiah 49:15). He has kept that word in his Son. The God who would not forget his children came and fed them with himself, the living bread given for the life of the world (John 6:51).

Is it right for a male apostle to call himself a nursing mother? Yes, and it is beautiful. Scripture uses mother imagery for God’s own tenderness (Isaiah 66:13), and Jesus longed to gather Jerusalem as a hen gathers her chicks (Matthew 23:37). Paul uses it to show the tenderness every true shepherd needs, not to blur the callings of men and women. (This commentary reads 1 Timothy 2:12 and 3:1–7 as giving the office of elder to qualified men; many faithful Christians read them differently, and the point here does not depend on it.) No shepherd is meant to be cold: authority in the church is the self-giving care of a mother at night as well as the steady formation of a father.

I am not a pastor. How do I share my life as well as the gospel? Open your ordinary life to people. Invite someone into your home, not just to an event. Let them see you pray, fail, apologise and keep trusting. Spend time with a younger believer, a lonely neighbour or a new member over months, not minutes. Most people are not won or grown by programmes but by a Christian who lets them close enough to see Christ at work.

Uncertain wording. “Affectionately desirous” translates homeiromai, found nowhere else in the New Testament and known elsewhere chiefly from a gravestone where grieving parents use it, it seems, of a lost child. Its exact shade cannot be fixed, but the sense of tender longing is clear.

Textual note. The Greek manuscripts divide between ēpioi, gentle, and nēpioi, infants, one letter apart, as the ESV footnote notes. Several of the earliest read infants, and some modern Bibles (the NIV) follow them; then Paul says he became like a small child among them, without airs or demands, before shifting to the nursing mother. Either reading tells against the charge of self-importance, and the ESV’s gentle gives the smoother sense.

verseByVerse.quote: For you remember, brothers, our labor and toil: we worked night and day, that we might not be a burden to any of you, while we proclaimed to you the gospel of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul worked exhausting hours at his trade so that he could preach the gospel to them without charging anyone a penny. It is the most solid evidence in the chapter.

Labour and toil. Kopos is labour to the point of exhaustion; mochthos is hardship, the grind. Paul is describing being tired.

We worked night and day. The trade was probably the tentmaking or leatherworking Luke mentions in Corinth (Acts 18:3; 20:34): heavy work gentlemen despised, at the bench before dawn and after dark, with the preaching fitted around it. Philippi also sent him gifts while he was in Thessalonica (Philippians 4:16), and even with that help he worked. The Son of God worked with his hands in a carpenter’s shop at Nazareth, and Paul followed him to a leatherworker’s bench at Thessalonica.

Not a burden to any of you. Instead of making demands (v. 6), he paid his own way, so as not to burden a poor young church or give ground to the charge of greed. A man running a religious racket does not work a double shift to avoid taking his converts’ money, and they had seen him come to the meeting with his hands still rough from the workshop.

Free of charge. Paul’s hands earned bread so that his mouth could give away the bread of life without a price attached. The gospel is free because it has been paid for. Christ, though he was rich, became poor for our sake, so that by his poverty we might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9). A preacher who sold that news would misrepresent it, and a preacher who worked a double shift to give it away was preaching it with his hands.

Should my church pay its pastor, then? Yes, normally. Scripture says the labourer deserves his wages and that those who preach the gospel should get their living by the gospel (1 Timothy 5:17–18; 1 Corinthians 9:14). A paid pastor is not less spiritual than a self-supporting one; Paul’s choice in Thessalonica was a freedom he used for a reason, not a rule for every church. Churches should support their ministers generously, and ministers should guard their hearts against loving money.

Does ordinary work matter to God? Very much. For Paul the workshop was not a distraction from real ministry but part of his witness. Your job, done honestly and well, is service to Christ (Colossians 3:23–24), provides for your family and the needy (4:11–12; Ephesians 4:28), and gives you daily contact with people who need the gospel. You need not leave work to serve God; you serve him there.
verseByVerse.note: Paul supported himself by his trade — he was a tentmaker.

verseByVerse.quote: You are witnesses, and God also, how holy and righteous and blameless was our conduct toward you believers. For you know how, like a father with his children, we exhorted each one of you and encouraged you and charged you to walk in a manner worthy of God, who calls you into his own kingdom and glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s conduct among them was beyond reproach, and like a father he trained each of them to live in a way that fits the God who is calling them into his kingdom and glory.

You are witnesses, and God also. Again two witnesses, the church and God (v. 5). “Holy” means devoted to God, “righteous” just toward people, “blameless” giving no one grounds for a charge. Paul claims not sinlessness but that no accusation would stick, which they could check. And he lived knowing that God watched the workshop and the private house as closely as the synagogue: God sees the hours no one else sees.

Like a father. The nursing mother (v. 7) carried warmth and self-giving; the father in the ancient household was responsible for teaching and training the child, and so for what the child became.

Exhorted, encouraged, charged. Exhorted (parakaleō): coming alongside to urge. Encouraged (paramytheomai): putting heart into someone. Charged (martyromai): solemnly insisting, so that the hearer knows he is answerable. A father who only encourages raises children who cannot stand; one who only charges raises children who leave. God himself never only scolds and never only soothes, but trains his children for glory.

Each one of you. In perhaps a month, while also working night and day at a bench, Paul dealt with these people individually, as he later did house to house in Ephesus (Acts 20:20).

To walk in a manner worthy of God. Worthy is not a standard they must reach to earn something. It means fitting: conduct that fits who God is and what has happened to you, as a uniform fits the service you are in.

Who calls you into his own kingdom and glory. The calling is present and ongoing, toward the kingdom and glory that are their destination. That is Paul’s whole method of motivation: not “behave, or else”, but “this is where you are going; live like someone going there”.

The glory is Christ’s. What is the glory God calls them into? Paul answers in his second letter: they were called through the gospel to obtain the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ (2 Thessalonians 2:14), and those he called he also glorified, conformed to the image of his Son (Romans 8:29–30). So the walk worthy of God looks like Jesus: “whoever says he abides in him ought to walk in the same way in which he walked” (1 John 2:6).

What is God’s kingdom and glory, and am I in it now? God’s kingdom is his saving rule through Christ. It has already begun: believers have been transferred into the kingdom of his beloved Son (Colossians 1:13). But its full glory, a share in God’s own splendour in the life of the age to come, waits for Christ’s return (Romans 8:18). So you are in it now, and you are being called further into it: a citizen already, walking toward the capital.

What does living worthy of God look like on an ordinary day? The life Paul describes in chapters 4 and 5: sexual purity, brotherly love, quiet honest work, hope at the graveside, alertness, respect for leaders, patience with the weak, joy, prayer and thanksgiving: not a special religious mood but ordinary life brought under the King. When you are unsure what to do, ask what fits a child of God on the way to his glory.

verseByVerse.ref: 2:13–16 – How They Received the Word — and What It Cost
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The message that converted them was God’s own word, and what it cost them shows it. They welcomed it not as human opinion but as God speaking, and it is still at work in them (v. 13). The proof is that they held on when their own countrymen turned against them, as the churches of Judea had done before them (v. 14). Paul then speaks severely of those who killed the Lord and the prophets and tried to keep the gospel from the Gentiles: words of covenant rebuke about the persecutors, not a race, which must be read with care and within their limits (vv. 15–16).
verseByVerse.theology:
Scripture as God’s own speech

Verse 13 is one of the clearest statements in the New Testament of what Scripture is (see the note on v. 13).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Verses 15–16 have been misused across the centuries; how to read them, and their limits, is treated at vv. 15–16.

Now: The wrath of verse 16 must be read beside 1:10 (see the end of the note on vv. 15–16).

verseByVerse.quote: And we also thank God constantly for this, that when you received the word of God, which you heard from us, you accepted it not as the word of men but as what it really is, the word of God, which is at work in you believers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul thanks God that they welcomed his preaching not as human opinion but as what it truly is, the word of God, which is now at work in them.

In the flow. Verses 1 to 12 defended the messengers; now Paul turns to the message, thanking God a second time. Had he been a fraud, his word would be suspect too; but they had heard God in it, and kept believing when it cost them their neighbours (vv. 14–16).

Received and accepted. They received it (paralambanō), the ordinary term for taking delivery of something; then they accepted it (dechomai), the word for welcoming a guest into your house. The first is hearing; the second is embracing. Plenty of people do the first every Sunday and never do the second.

What it really is. They heard it from a leatherworker with marks on his back, in a city full of competing lecturers. Nothing about the messenger suggested it, yet they concluded God was addressing them, and Paul says they were right.

At work in you. The verb (energeō, the root of our word energy) is present and continuous: the word is working in them while Paul writes (Hebrews 4:12; Isaiah 55:11). The same voice that said “Let there be light” speaks in Scripture and makes dead hearts live.

Hearing the Lord in his messengers. Jesus had told his apostles, “The one who hears you hears me, and the one who rejects you rejects me” (Luke 10:16). The Thessalonians heard a leatherworker and met the risen Christ, because the apostolic word is the word of Christ (Colossians 3:16), and his sheep hear their shepherd’s voice in it (John 10:27). When you read this letter, you are not merely weighing Paul’s argument; the Lord himself is addressing you, and you are answering him.

The decision every hearer makes. Every hearer decides what the Bible is, usually without noticing. If it is a valuable human document, you weigh it, keep what persuades you, and remain the judge. If it is the word of God, the position is reversed: it judges you. There is no third option where it is God’s word and you still decide which parts to keep.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every preacher’s words are God’s word. Only as preaching faithfully conveys Scripture does it carry God’s authority.

How can a book written by men be God’s word? Because God spoke through them, not around them. He used their personalities, languages, research and circumstances, and so superintended their writing that what they wrote is exactly what he intended to say (2 Peter 1:21). Paul wrote as Paul, and the Thessalonians were still right to hear God. The human and divine are no more rivals in Scripture than in Christ, who is fully human and fully God.

Is it not circular to believe the Bible is God’s word because the Bible says so? Every final authority has to vouch for itself, or it would not be final; whoever trusts reason alone can only defend reason by reasoning. The Thessalonians were not argued into faith by a clever proof. They heard the word, and it did what only God’s word does: it showed them their idols, set Christ before them, and changed them. The Spirit himself convinces people that Scripture is God’s word as they hear it, through its message, not apart from it (Westminster 1.5; 1689 1.5). There are good reasons too: the resurrection of Jesus, and his own trust in the Scriptures (John 10:35). But in the end God’s word is believed the way the sun is seen: by its own light. An honest doubter is not a fool for asking; the invitation is the one the Thessalonians accepted, to hear it and see what it does.

How do I receive the word as God’s word when I read it? Come expecting God to speak, not merely to gather information. Pray for open eyes. Read to obey, not just to understand: ask what it shows you of God and Christ, what it promises and commands, and what you must believe or change. When it contradicts you, let it win. And keep coming back: the word works over time, like seed, not usually like lightning.

What about new revelations or prophecies today? The word that works in believers is the apostolic word, now complete in Scripture. The canon is closed: God has spoken finally in his Son (Hebrews 1:1–2), and the apostles’ teaching is the church’s foundation (Ephesians 2:20). Impressions and promptings must be tested by Scripture and never placed beside it; everything we need for life and godliness is already given there.

Where Christians differ: is Scripture the word of God? Some say the Bible contains or becomes the word of God, or is merely human testimony. This commentary’s view: The apostles’ message, now written in Scripture, is what it really is: the word of God, not merely the words of men, though spoken through men. Scripture is God-breathed and authoritative in all it affirms (2 Timothy 3:16; 2 Peter 1:21), as the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession confess (Westminster 1.4; 1689 1.4). Its authority does not depend on human acceptance; it is God’s word whether received or not, and it works in those who believe.

verseByVerse.quote: For you, brothers, became imitators of the churches of God in Christ Jesus that are in Judea. For you suffered the same things from your own countrymen as they did from the Jews,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Their suffering at the hands of their own people is not a sign that something has gone wrong; it puts them in line with the first churches in Judea.

Imitators of the churches in Judea. Congregations nearly a thousand miles away that they had never met, whom they imitate by enduring persecution as the first churches had.

Your own countrymen. The Judean believers were opposed by fellow Jews (Acts 8:1–3; 12:1–3); the Thessalonian believers by fellow Thessalonians, stirred up by some of the synagogue (Acts 17:5–9). In each case the opposition came from their own neighbours, which hurts most. These Gentiles had walked out of the guild dinners, household shrines and civic festivals, and the pressure came from employers, families and old friends.

Joining a line. A young church under attack asks in the night whether something has gone wrong. Paul’s answer: they have joined a line with the oldest churches. Their suffering is not evidence that they took a wrong turn but that they are on the right road.

The road their Lord walked first. The line goes back further: their suffering was Christ’s before it was theirs. “He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him” (John 1:11); even his brothers did not believe in him (John 7:5). And he told his disciples to expect the same: “if they persecuted me, they will also persecute you” (John 15:20). The Thessalonians were walking in his footprints, and those footprints lead through a cross to an empty tomb.

The Head feels every blow. When Saul of Tarsus was dragging believers out of their houses, the risen Lord stopped him on the road and asked, Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? (Acts 9:4). No believer pushed out of a guild or a family suffers out of his sight; and the voice that asked that question turned the persecutor into a brother.

What it does not mean. It does not mean persecution proves a church true: plenty of people are disliked for being disagreeable. But faithful churches should expect it (2 Timothy 3:12), and opposition is not proof of failure either, which is what the frightened heart assumes at three in the morning.

My own family opposes my faith. What should I do? You are in good company: Jesus said a person’s enemies may be those of his own household (Matthew 10:36). Stay loving, respectful and patient, and serve your family in every way that does not require disobeying Christ. Do not argue constantly; let your life speak, and speak when asked. Keep praying for them, and find support in your church family. And where there is any threat of harm, seek help and safety; enduring hostility is not the same as tolerating abuse.

Why does it help to know others suffer the same? Because suffering isolates and lies: it says you are alone, and that God has abandoned you. Knowing that Christians across the world and down the centuries have walked this road answers both lies: you belong to a family that has always suffered and always been kept. So pray for and learn about the persecuted church today: they strengthen us, and we can strengthen them.

verseByVerse.quote: who killed both the Lord Jesus and the prophets, and drove us out, and displease God and oppose all mankind by hindering us from speaking to the Gentiles that they might be saved—so as always to fill up the measure of their sins. But wrath has come upon them at last!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who killed the Lord and the prophets, and are now trying to stop the gospel reaching the Gentiles, stand under God’s judgment. This hardest passage in the letter has been misused across the centuries to justify appalling things, so it must be read carefully and its limits stated plainly.

Who killed both the Lord Jesus and the prophets. Paul is himself a Jew, a Hebrew of Hebrews (Philippians 3:5), who insists in Romans that God has not rejected his people (Romans 11:1). Whatever this passage means, it cannot mean what Romans denies. His target is specific, and he names their actions: the leaders who rejected Christ and handed him over, following a long pattern of killing the prophets (Matthew 23:29–37; Acts 7:52).

The language of covenant rebuke. The charge sheet is drawn from Israel’s own Scriptures: the prophets said harder things about their nation’s leaders than Paul does here, and Jesus lamented over Jerusalem as the city that kills the prophets (Matthew 23:37). This is how God’s covenant people were rebuked from within, by one of their own. It becomes something else entirely when outsiders pick it up as a weapon.

And drove us out. From Thessalonica and then from Beroea (Acts 17:5–10, 13), a few months earlier.

Oppose all mankind. It sounds sweeping, but it is aimed at one thing: stopping the gospel from reaching the nations, which harms the whole human race. It is a charge about the mission, not about race. Why they hindered it is plain: Paul was drawing God-fearing Gentiles away from the synagogue and offering them Israel’s covenant blessings without circumcision or the law, which looked to his opponents like a betrayal of Israel. Luke says simply that they were jealous (Acts 17:4–5).

Fill up the measure. As God waited until the sin of the Amorites was complete (Genesis 15:16), and as Jesus told the leaders of his day to fill up the measure of their fathers (Matthew 23:32), so these opponents were filling up their sins to the point of judgment. God’s patience is long, and it has an end.

Wrath has come. The verb is past: judgment is so certain that Paul can speak of it as already arrived, as the prophets often did. Within twenty years Jerusalem and the temple would fall (AD 70).

Our sins were in their hands. The Lord Jesus was killed by the hands of lawless men, and our sins were in their hands. And from the cross he prayed, “Father, forgive them” (Luke 23:34, a prayer missing from some early manuscripts but widely received as genuine). The wrath opposition to God deserves fell on him, so that persecutors like Saul could be made apostles, and enemies like us sons.

What it does not mean. It does not mean all Jews are under wrath, or that Jews alone killed Jesus. Gentiles shared in it (Acts 4:27), and our sins put him there.

The passage ends where the letter began. Wrath is what Jesus delivers people from (1:10), Paul among them, once a persecutor hindering the gospel. Opposition to the gospel places anyone, Jew or Gentile, under the wrath the gospel exists to save them from, and the same gospel stands open to them. The opponents were not irreligious men but zealous ones, as Paul had been (Galatians 1:13–14). Religion used to earn a standing with God can make a person the fiercest enemy of grace, because grace tells him his record counts for nothing. A sober warning is not a licence for contempt, and anyone who has used this passage for contempt has read the man who wrote Romans 11 exactly backwards.

How should I treat people who oppose the gospel? Pray for them, love them, and keep telling them the truth, as Paul spent his life preaching to the opponents he describes. You were once an enemy of God yourself (Romans 5:10), and the fiercest opponent of the church in that generation became its greatest missionary. Leave judgment to God, and never return hatred for hatred.

Does this passage settle what God will do with Israel in the future? No. It describes the judgment on those rejecting Christ and blocking the gospel in Paul’s own day. Whether Romans 11 promises a large-scale turning of the Jewish people to Christ before the end is a question on which faithful Reformed Christians differ, and this verse does not decide it. Every view agrees that Jewish people, like everyone, are saved only through faith in Jesus the Messiah, and that the church should pray for their salvation, as Paul did.

Did Paul write these verses? A few scholars think these verses were added later, because they sound so harsh and seem to look back on the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70. But no manuscript lacks them (see the introduction), and they fit Paul’s own experience of being driven out by Jewish opponents (Acts 17:5, 13).

Where Christians differ: is this anti-Jewish? Some say this passage is anti-Semitic, or that it was not written by Paul. This commentary’s view: Paul, himself a Jew, is speaking of those who opposed the gospel, not of the Jewish people as a whole. He loved his people deeply and longed for their salvation (Romans 9:1–5; 10:1), and many of the first believers were Jews. His language echoes Jesus and the prophets, who spoke similarly to Israel. Christians must never use this passage to justify hatred of Jews, which is a terrible sin that has stained church history.

Uncertain wording. “At last” translates eis telos, which can mean at last, fully, or for ever. Nor is it certain what “has come” points to: a recent disaster in Judea, the judgment already begun in their rejection of Christ, or the final judgment spoken of as done. The likely sense is that God’s judgment has overtaken them fully and decisively.
verseByVerse.note: Paul, himself a Jew, is speaking of those who opposed the gospel, as he had once done — not of every Jewish person.

parallels.desc: the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete

verseByVerse.ref: 2:17–20 – Orphaned From Them, and What He Expects to Hold
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul did not abandon them; he was torn from them, and they are what he hopes to hold when Jesus comes. He felt the separation like a bereavement and tried again and again to return, but Satan blocked the way (vv. 17–18). Yet his heart has never left them, for they are his hope, joy and crown of boasting before the Lord Jesus at his coming (vv. 19–20).
verseByVerse.theology:
The coming, and the pastor’s wreath

The reward of pastoral work is not the admiration of the present age but the sight, on that day, of people standing before Jesus because the gospel was faithfully preached and patiently tended.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The enemy who blocked Paul’s road did not win (see the note on vv. 17–18).

Now: On the last day, what do you expect to show: a record of what you achieved, or people who are standing there because you served them?

verseByVerse.quote: But since we were torn away from you, brothers, for a short time, in person not in heart, we endeavored the more eagerly and with great desire to see you face to face, because we wanted to come to you—I, Paul, again and again—but Satan hindered us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul did not abandon them: he was torn away against his will, longed to see them, and tried again and again to come back, but Satan blocked the way.

Torn away. The word is built on the word for orphan (aporphanisthentes). Having called himself their mother and father, Paul is now the bereaved one. And his departure was forced (Acts 17:10); he did not abandon them, as his critics said.

For a short time, in person not in heart. Two phrases keep the grief from despair: the separation is brief, and it is bodily only.

The more eagerly. Opponents said he did not care; being torn away made him try harder.

I, Paul, again and again. He interrupts his own plural to sign his name: he tried, personally and repeatedly.

Satan hindered us. Hindered (enkoptō) means to block, as by breaking up a road. Paul does not say how: it may have been the money the authorities took from Jason as security (Acts 17:9), which made his return dangerous for his hosts, or illness, or hostility elsewhere. He read it as the work of an enemy keeping a young church from its teacher.

Hold it with care, in both directions. Not every delay is a demonic assault, but Paul did not think his blocked plans were mere bad luck. Satan can hinder our plans, but only within God’s permission, as with Job; and Paul never says Satan won. Timothy went instead (3:2), and the letter you are reading was written because Paul could not come. In the end it was Satan who was hindered. At the cross Satan did his worst, and it became the salvation of the world.

Not left as orphans. The orphan word recalls a promise. On the night before he died, Jesus told his disciples, “I will not leave you as orphans; I will come to you” (John 14:18), speaking of the Spirit who would be with them for ever. The apostle could be kept away; the Lord could not.

How can I tell whether Satan is hindering me or God is closing a door? Often you cannot tell, and need not. Paul read one blocked road as Satan’s work and another as the Spirit’s (Acts 16:6–7), and in both he did the same thing: trusted God, kept praying, and did what he could. Ask whether the plan was clearly good and in line with Scripture, and keep seeking it by lawful means. If the door stays shut, accept it from God’s hand, and look for the other way he may be opening, as Timothy went when Paul could not.

Is it right to grieve over separation from Christian friends? Yes. Paul felt it like bereavement and was not ashamed to say so; Christian love is meant to be strong enough to hurt when we are parted. Bring the ache to God, keep in touch as you can (Paul wrote a letter and sent a friend), and remember that every separation between believers is for a short time. There is a day of reunion that no road-block can stop.

Where Christians differ: Satan’s power over circumstances. Some blame Satan for every difficulty; others ignore him. This commentary’s view: Satan is real and does oppose God’s work, sometimes through circumstances (Job 1–2; 2 Corinthians 12:7). But he acts only within the limits God permits, and God overrules even his opposition for good (Romans 8:28). Elsewhere Luke tells us the Spirit prevented Paul from going somewhere (Acts 16:6–7). Discernment is needed, and in every case we trust God’s sovereign providence, as the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession teach (Westminster 5.4; 1689 5.4).

verseByVerse.quote: For what is our hope or joy or crown of boasting before our Lord Jesus at his coming? Is it not you? For you are our glory and joy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What Paul hopes to hold up with joy when the Lord Jesus comes is not his own achievement but these very people.

For what is our hope or joy or crown of boasting? Accused of chasing glory (v. 6), Paul now says what he is actually after: the people he is writing to. He asks it as a question and answers it himself, which is warmer than a statement.

Crown. The stephanos is the winner’s wreath at the games, also presented when a king or emperor visited.

At his coming. Coming (parousia) meant in ordinary Greek the state visit of a sovereign to one of his cities, when the citizens streamed out to meet him on the road and escorted him in (see the introduction).

Is it not you? So the picture is this: the King arrives, and Paul is standing there, and what he has to show is not a record of his labours but a group of people. Their being there is the wreath. And they are his glory and joy now as well as on that day (Philippians 4:1), which settles the accusation better than any denial: a man seeking glory from people uses them and moves on.

The joy set before him. The King is coming, and his people will go out to meet him. On that day every faithful labour will be seen for what it was. For Christ, too, has a joy set before him: the people his Father gave him, brought home. Glory to the coming King.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul’s salvation depended on them. His hope of eternal life rested on Christ alone; they will be the joy and fruit of his labour.

Will Christians receive rewards in heaven? Yes. Scripture speaks of crowns and rewards given by Christ (1 Corinthians 3:12–14; 2 Timothy 4:8), not earning salvation, which is a free gift, but as the Father’s gracious recognition of what his children did by his grace: God crowns his own works in us. And the greatest reward is not a thing but a joy: to see Christ, and to see with him the people we loved and served for his sake.

Will we recognise one another when Christ comes? Paul expects to stand with these very people before the Lord, and Scripture never suggests we lose who we are in glory. The disciples recognised Moses and Elijah, and the risen Jesus was known by his friends. Paul will build on this in chapter 4, where the dead and the living are brought together to meet the Lord. Christian love is not ended by death; it is gathered up into the joy of his coming.

keyVerse.quote: just as we have been approved by God to be entrusted with the gospel, so we speak, not to please man, but to please God who tests our hearts.
keyVerse.note: This is the governing idea of Paul’s defence. Because the gospel is God’s, entrusted to him, he cannot flatter, profit or seek glory from it; because God tests his heart, he can be both bold and gentle. It is also the reason the Thessalonians were right to hear his message as the word of God (v. 13).

2.reflection:
Paul defends himself by pointing to things the Thessalonians could check: his courage, his motives, his hard work, his gentleness (vv. 1–12). What marks should we look for in those who teach us, and how do they help us tell a true ministry from a false one?

Paul shared “not only the gospel of God but also our own selves” (v. 8). Who has done that for you? What would it look like for you to share your life, and not only your words, with someone this month?

The Thessalonians received the message “not as the word of men but as what it really is, the word of God” (v. 13). In practice, what is the difference between treating the Bible as a valuable human book and treating it as God speaking to you?

Paul says his hope, joy and crown at the Lord’s coming are people (vv. 19–20). How would it change your goals, your work or your church involvement if you measured them by that day?

3.title: Standing Firm in the Lord
3.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 3 completes the backward-looking half of the letter. Having told of his longing to return (2:17–20), Paul now tells what he did when he could not come and what happened next, and ends with a prayer that opens the teaching of chapters 4 and 5.

The message. God keeps his suffering people, through means: a brother sent, truth taught in advance, prayer night and day. Affliction for Christ is not a sign that the plan has failed; it is where God has placed his people, and a church standing fast in the Lord there is the very life of those who love it. Yet what they need most is a work of God within them: overflowing love, and hearts made firm and holy for the day Jesus comes.

Why it was said. Driven out after a few weeks, Paul had left converts under fierce pressure, and Satan had blocked every attempt to return (2:14–18; see the introduction). He did not know whether the church still stood or whether the tempter had used the suffering to coax them back.

How the chapter makes its case. First, the sending (vv. 1–5): unable to bear the silence, Paul stays alone in Athens and sends Timothy to steady them, reminding them that they are “destined for” the affliction he had foretold. Then the news (vv. 6–10): Timothy brings good news of their faith and love, and the distressed apostle says, “now we live”; his joy runs over into thanks and earnest prayer. Last, the prayer (vv. 11–13), to the Father and the Lord Jesus together: for a road back, for love that overflows, and for hearts blameless in holiness at Christ’s coming, the agenda for the rest of the letter.

Where it leads. Timothy is sent to establish them, but it is the Lord who establishes hearts (v. 13). The church stands “in the Lord” (v. 8), held in the hand from which no one can snatch them. Paul prays to Jesus as to the Father, and applies to him, without comment, the prophet’s picture of the LORD coming with all his holy ones. The chapter ends where the letter keeps arriving: before God, at the coming of our Lord Jesus, blameless because of him.

For us. Expect affliction for Christ and do not read it as abandonment. Care for struggling believers as Paul did, by going, sending, writing and praying. And ask God, before you try harder, for the love and holiness only he can give.

verseByVerse.ref: 3:1–5 – Timothy Sent, and Suffering as a Posting
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Suffering for Christ is no accident, and a church under it must be steadied, not left alone. Unable to bear the silence, Paul stays alone in Athens and sends Timothy to make the young believers firm (vv. 1–2), so that no one is unsettled by afflictions which God had appointed and Paul had warned them of (vv. 3–4). Behind it all lies his fear that the tempter had used their suffering to undo his work (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology:
Affliction as appointment, not accident

Suffering for the gospel is something God has appointed for his people, not an accident (see the note on v. 3), and he makes such suffering purposeful, producing endurance, character and hope (Romans 5:3–4).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul feared not only that persecution would smash this church but that it would coax them gently back to their old life (v. 3).

Now: Honest preparation for hardship is a form of pastoral care, and leaving it out is no kindness (v. 4).

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore when we could bear it no longer, we were willing to be left behind at Athens alone, and we sent Timothy, our brother and God's coworker in the gospel of Christ, to establish and exhort you in your faith,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Unable to bear not knowing how they were, Paul gave up his only companion and sent Timothy back to make the young church firm.

Could bear it no longer. To bear (stegō) is to hold out, as a roof holds out rain. Paul says it twice in five verses (vv. 1, 5): that is what the months had been like.

Left behind at Athens alone. In Athens he was mocked for mentioning resurrection and made few converts (Acts 17:15–34), and there he sent away his companion. Paul, whose letters are full of names, chose isolation because a frightened congregation needed someone more than he did. This is what sharing “our own selves” (2:8) cost him.

Filling a gap in Acts. Acts mentions only that Silas and Timothy were told to join Paul at Athens (17:15) and later reached him at Corinth (18:5). This verse fills the gap: Timothy probably reached Athens, and Paul sent him straight back north to the church he could not reach himself (2:18).

God’s coworker. A startling title for a young man. In the gospel God does not merely employ his servants but works alongside them: “we are God’s fellow workers” (1 Corinthians 3:9).

To establish and exhort. To establish (stērizō) is to make firm, as you might prop up a leaning wall; to exhort (parakaleō) is to come alongside and urge. Both aim at stability: when a church is under attack, the first task is to keep it standing.

The Lord who establishes. Timothy was sent to do what only the Lord can finally do: Paul prays that God would establish their hearts (3:13), and later writes that the Lord is faithful and will establish them (2 Thessalonians 3:3). Timothy was the means; the one holding up the leaning wall was the risen Christ, who said, “I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matthew 16:18).

Alone so that they would not be. Paul’s choice echoes a greater one. The Son of God let every friend leave him so that his people would never be left: you will leave me alone, he told them, yet I am not alone, for the Father is with me (John 16:32). Because he was deserted, not one of his own is ever abandoned. And he lets ordinary believers share the work as his coworkers.

If God keeps his people, why was Paul so anxious? Because God keeps his people through means, and Paul was one of them. Trust in God’s sovereignty made him pray and send, not sit still. His was the anxiety of love, not of unbelief, and he did with it what love should do: he acted, and brought it to God. Your concern for a struggling believer may be God’s way of moving you to be the help he intends.

What does following up a new believer actually involve? What Timothy did: going to them, strengthening their grasp of the truth, urging them on, and preparing them for trouble. In practice: meeting, reading the Bible and praying together, answering questions, introducing them to other believers, noticing when they go quiet. It needs no title, only time, patience and love, and it is some of the most fruitful work in the church.

Textual note. Some manuscripts read “God’s servant” instead of God’s coworker, as the ESV footnote notes, probably because copyists found the bolder title surprising.

verseByVerse.quote: that no one be moved by these afflictions. For you yourselves know that we are destined for this.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Suffering for Christ is no sign that something has gone wrong; it is where God has placed his people. His fear was that they might be coaxed, not crushed, out of the faith.

That no one be moved. Moved (sainō) was first used of a dog wagging its tail, so to fawn or coax, and later to unsettle. Faith is seldom lost in dramatic renunciation, but by erosion: the family who keep asking, the invitation it is easier to accept, the guild dinner it costs too much to refuse. A wagging tail, not a battering ram.

Destined for this. We are laid, set in place (keimetha), as Paul was set in prison for the defence of the gospel (Philippians 1:16). Affliction has not slipped past God; it is where he has placed them (John 16:33; 2 Timothy 3:12). What steadies a shaken believer is not being told the trouble will stop but that it is no mistake. If suffering means the plan has gone wrong, every hard week is evidence against the faith; if God has laid you there, the hard week proves only that you are where he put you.

Appointed first for Christ. Christ was the first to be placed on this road. On the way to Emmaus the risen Lord asked, “Was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory?” (Luke 24:26). His suffering was no accident God repaired afterwards but the appointed road, with glory at its end. What was appointed for the Head is appointed for his body: “through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God” (Acts 14:22). The road may be hard, but Christ walks it with his people, and it ends at his throne.

In everyday life. Notice where you are being nudged away from Christ: the joke you laugh along with, the habit quietly resumed, the conviction you no longer mention. Name it before God, who forgives and does not let go of you, and stand where he has placed you.

Does “destined for this” apply to all suffering, or only persecution? Paul means suffering for the gospel, but the principle reaches further: nothing comes to God’s children by accident, whether illness, loss or disappointment, and he works all of it for their good (Romans 8:28). That does not make every hardship good in itself, nor forbid you to seek relief. Pray for healing, seek justice, take the medicine, knowing that your Father has placed you where you are and has not lost track of you.

Is it wrong to try to avoid persecution? Not in itself. Jesus told his disciples to flee from one town to the next (Matthew 10:23), and Paul left Thessalonica and Damascus by night. You may leave, keep a low profile, or use the law’s protection, as Paul used his citizenship. What is wrong is avoiding it by denying Christ or compromising obedience: you may not lie about him, worship what he forbids, or abandon his people to save yourself.

verseByVerse.quote: For when we were with you, we kept telling you beforehand that we were to suffer affliction, just as it has come to pass, and just as you know. For this reason, when I could bear it no longer, I sent to learn about your faith, for fear that somehow the tempter had tempted you and our labor would be in vain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul had warned them from the start that trouble would come, and when it came he feared the tempter would use it to undo his work.

We kept telling you beforehand. With only a few weeks, Paul kept telling them: this will cost you. Honest evangelism tells people the cost (Luke 14:28), and it pays: a church told the truth in advance meets hardship saying, he said this would happen; a church promised an easy road meets it asking whether the whole thing was false.

I sent. The plural becomes singular: Paul admits his own fear, unembarrassed.

The tempter. Satan’s title in the wilderness (Matthew 4:3), where his tactic was suggestion, not violence. Having blocked Paul’s road (2:18), he works on the church: keep the teacher away, then use suffering to tempt believers to give up.

In vain. Empty (kenos), the word of 2:1, where Paul was sure his visit had not been empty; here he admits the fear beneath that confidence. The apostle so certain about election in chapter 1 also lay awake fearing his work had come to nothing, and neither cancels the other. Strong faith is not the absence of anxiety.

The tempter has met his match. Paul knew the tempter’s methods, and who had beaten him. In the wilderness the Lord Jesus faced the same voice, hungry and alone, and answered every suggestion with the word of God (Matthew 4:1–11). Because he himself has suffered when tempted, he is able to help those who are being tempted (Hebrews 2:18). The church faced a defeated enemy.

What it does not mean. Not that true believers can be lost. Paul feared their faith might prove false, and his labour fruitless; Timothy’s report proved it genuine.

If true believers cannot be lost, why did Paul fear? Because he could see only their profession, not their hearts, and some who make a start fall away because their faith was never real (Matthew 13:20–21; 1 John 2:19). God’s elect will persevere (John 10:28–29; Philippians 1:6), but by means: warnings, teaching, encouragement, prayer, and Paul’s fear moved him to supply them. So we hold both: unshakeable confidence in God’s keeping, and earnest care that no one drifts. And if you fear that the falling away describes you, the fear is itself a hopeful sign: those whose faith was never real seldom lie awake over it. Bring it to Christ, who keeps all who come to him (John 6:37).

How do I tell people the cost without frightening them away? Tell the truth with the reward in view. Jesus never hid the cost of discipleship, and never mentioned it without the treasure: whoever loses his life for my sake will find it (Matthew 16:25). Say plainly that following Christ may cost friendships, comfort and reputation; then say why it is worth it: forgiveness, adoption, a living hope, Christ himself.

verseByVerse.ref: 3:6–13 – The News From Home, and a Prayer for Love
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A church standing fast in the Lord is the joy and life of those who love it, and the right response is thanks and prayer. Timothy’s good news of their faith and love revives the distressed apostle (vv. 6–8); his joy becomes thanksgiving and earnest prayer to come and complete what their faith lacks (vv. 9–10). He then prays to the Father and the Lord Jesus together for a road back, for overflowing love, and for hearts blameless in holiness at Christ’s coming (vv. 11–13), the themes of the chapters to come.
verseByVerse.theology:
Two persons, one verb

In verse 11 Paul names the Father and the Lord Jesus together with a singular verb (see the note on v. 11).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: What was lacking in their faith was not sincerity but completeness (see the note on vv. 9–10).

Now: Paul prays that a persecuted church would overflow in love “for all” (see the note on vv. 12–13).

verseByVerse.quote: But now that Timothy has come to us from you, and has brought us the good news of your faith and love and reported that you always remember us kindly and long to see us, as we long to see you— for this reason, brothers, in all our distress and affliction we have been comforted about you through your faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Timothy’s report that their faith and love were holding, and that they still loved Paul, comforted the apostle in his own distress.

Now that Timothy has come. The mood changes. Timothy had rejoined Paul in Corinth (Acts 18:5), and this letter was written in the first glow of his report.

Good news. The verb is Paul’s word for preaching the gospel (euangelizomai), used only here in his letters of anything else. News that a church was standing was, to him, gospel news. It answered three fears. Their faith: they had not been coaxed away. Their love: they had not turned on each other. And they remembered him kindly: the slanders had not worked.

Comforted about you. The apostle is comforted by the young converts. In Corinth he was in weakness and fear and much trembling (1 Corinthians 2:3), and the Lord had to tell him in a vision not to be afraid (Acts 18:9–10). The help runs both ways: those who strengthen others are held up when the believers they worry about keep going. If you wonder whether your quiet faithfulness matters to anyone, this kind of faithfulness was what got Paul through Corinth.

Comfort that flows through Christ. “As we share abundantly in Christ’s sufferings, so through Christ we share abundantly in comfort too” (2 Corinthians 1:5). Their faith was Christ’s gift, and so was the comfort: Christ comforts his servants by keeping his people.

A young man coming down the road. “How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news” (Isaiah 52:7). God sent such feet to a frightened apostle in Corinth, with word that a church was still standing. Every such report is a small echo of the prophet’s great news, that our God reigns and has bared his holy arm to save (Isaiah 52:7–10), accomplished in his Son.

In everyday life. Send a word this week to a pastor, parent or mentor who has worried about you, and pass on good news of someone’s faith; it may be the best thing a weary servant hears all month.

Is it all right to care what people think of me? It is right to want your brothers and sisters to love you, and to grieve when slander damages that. What is wrong is letting their opinion govern your obedience (2:4). Paul would have preached the same gospel whether they thought well of him or not, but he was deeply glad that they did. Love wants to be loved back, and that is not vanity.

verseByVerse.quote: For now we live, if you are standing fast in the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s life is bound up with theirs: to know that they stand firm in the Lord makes him alive again. He does not say he is relieved but that he lives; the months of not knowing had been a kind of death.

Love makes you a hostage. This is not the unhealthy dependence of a leader whose identity rests on his people’s performance; Paul sought no glory from them (2:6). It is love: when you love someone, how you are depends on how they are. That is not a defect in love; it is what love is.

Standing fast. To stand firm (stēkō) suits a soldier holding his position in the line. Paul uses it repeatedly of churches under pressure (Philippians 1:27; 4:1). It means you were still there when the pushing stopped. The “if” is also a gentle encouragement: keep standing.

In the Lord. Not by willpower or loyalty to Paul: the place they held was a person, and their strength was his. He had said of his sheep that no one will snatch them out of his hand (John 10:28), and a church standing fast in the Lord is a church being held by him. He set his face to Jerusalem and did not turn back when every disciple fled. The life Paul felt at Timothy’s news is a small echo of the joy of the Good Shepherd, who rejoices over every sheep he keeps.

What does standing firm look like when I feel weak? It looks like still being there: not feeling strong, but not leaving your post. You keep praying when prayer is dry, keep gathering with God’s people when you would rather not, keep refusing the sin that keeps returning, and keep trusting Christ when you do not understand him. Because you stand in the Lord, your weakness does not decide the outcome. He holds the line with you.

verseByVerse.quote: For what thanksgiving can we return to God for you, for all the joy that we feel for your sake before our God, as we pray most earnestly night and day that we may see you face to face and supply what is lacking in your faith?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s joy over them is too great for any thanks he can offer God, and it drives him to pray night and day to come and complete what their faith still lacks.

What thanksgiving can we return to God for you? A real question, and Paul does not answer it: his joy is too large for words. And the thanks goes to God, since he is the one who kept them.

Most earnestly night and day. Far beyond measure, several words piled into one (hyperekperissou); and night and day, as he had worked at his trade (2:9).

Supply what is lacking in your faith. This is no rebuke; Paul has just spent eight verses celebrating their faith. The verb (katartizō) means to put a thing into working order: mending nets (Matthew 4:21), setting a bone, God equipping his people for every good work (Hebrews 13:21). What is lacking is not sincerity but completeness: the teaching he had no time to give in a few weeks. Chapters 4 and 5 begin to supply it.

Already full in Christ. What was lacking was not Christ. In him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily, Paul tells another young church, and you have been filled in him (Colossians 2:9–10). The gaps would be filled not by adding a technique, experience or teacher alongside Christ, but by knowing more of the Christ they already had. Growth in faith is growth into Christ, never beyond him. He mends what is torn and sets what is broken, and will not stop until his people are made whole in the image of his Son.

How do I know what is lacking in my faith? Some gaps are faults; others are simply an unfinished education, where nobody ever taught you, and Paul meets these not with reproach but with a longing to fill them in. So ask honestly: where do I not know what the Bible teaches? Where do I believe but not obey? Where does fear still rule? Then sit under faithful preaching, read whole books of Scripture, ask a mature believer for help, and pray. Gaps are expected; staying content with them is not.

Is my faith real if it has gaps? Yes. The Thessalonians had a famous faith (1:8) that still lacked things. Real faith is not perfect faith but faith that rests on Christ and wants to grow, and wanting the gaps filled is itself a sign of life.

verseByVerse.quote: Now may our God and Father himself, and our Lord Jesus, direct our way to you,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul prays to the Father and the Lord Jesus together to clear the road back to Thessalonica.

In the flow. Verses 11 to 13 close the first half of the letter and open the second. Paul asks for a clear road back (v. 11), overflowing love (v. 12) and hearts made holy for Christ’s coming (v. 13), and chapters 4 and 5 take up those themes: holiness (4:1–8), love (4:9–12) and the coming of the Lord (4:13–5:11). He prays first for what he is about to teach.

The Father and the Lord Jesus. Paul names two, yet the Greek verb “direct” is singular, as if for one. A prayer to the Father and the Son together assumes that the Son is God, and shows how early and naturally the highest view of Christ was in place.

Direct our way to you. Direct (kateuthynō) means to make straight, to clear a road, the opposite of Satan cutting into it (2:18). The enemy blocks roads, but God rules them, so Paul does not rebuke the devil; he asks God to clear the road, and gets on with what he can do from where he is.

No enemy can close what they open. The Father and the Son act as one, and rule every road on earth. The Lord Jesus addressed in this prayer is himself the way to the Father, and he has made the road to God straight for us by his blood. Every road his people travel, blocked or open, runs at last to his Father’s house.

What it does not mean. Not that the Father and the Son are one person; they are distinct persons who act as one God.

Is it right to pray to Jesus, or only to the Father? Both. The usual pattern is prayer to the Father, through the Son, by the Spirit (Ephesians 2:18), but Scripture also shows believers praying to Jesus directly: Stephen called on him as he died (Acts 7:59), Paul pleaded with the Lord about his thorn (2 Corinthians 12:8), and here he prays to the Father and the Son together. Because the Son is God, he may be prayed to and worshipped; you will not offend the Father by speaking to his Son.

What should I make of it when God does not answer my prayer the way I asked? Keep praying, and watch for what he does instead. Paul did not get his visit for years, but God answered the deeper request: the church was strengthened and Paul’s love reached them, through a letter. God gives his children what they would ask for if they knew what he knows. A no or a not yet from a wise Father is still an answer, and often a better one.

verseByVerse.quote: and may the Lord make you increase and abound in love for one another and for all, as we do for you, so that he may establish your hearts blameless in holiness before our God and Father, at the coming of our Lord Jesus with all his saints.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul asks the Lord to make their love overflow, to everyone, so that they will stand blameless and holy before God when Jesus comes.

Increase and abound in love. The verbs are extravagant. The first (pleonazō) means to multiply; the second (perisseuō) to overflow, like a river over its banks. He is asking for a flood, and his own affection, shown for two chapters, is the measure: “as we do for you”.

For one another and for all. The second phrase is the sharp one. A community under attack naturally turns inward; Paul prays that a persecuted church would overflow with love toward the very people making its life hard, persecutors included (Matthew 5:44).

Who produces it. May the Lord make you increase: Paul asks God to do it in them rather than telling them to try harder. The commands come in chapter 4, but the order is the order of all his letters: ask God for what you then go and work at.

Blameless in holiness. Establish is the propping-up word of verse 2 (stērizō): what Timothy was sent to do, Paul asks God to do. Blameless means without just accusation, before God at the judgment; holiness is being set apart for God and made like him. No small request, for the God before whom they will stand is the one the seraphim call holy, holy, holy (Isaiah 6:3), before whom even Isaiah cried that he was lost.

With all his saints. “Coming” is again parousia, Christ’s return. His saints, his holy ones, may be the angels who accompany him (Matthew 25:31), on the pattern of Zechariah 14:5, where the LORD comes and all the holy ones with him; or believers who have died, whom God will bring with him (4:14); or both. Paul has borrowed a prophet’s picture of the LORD arriving in judgment and applied it, without comment, to Jesus.

How can anyone be blameless before God? In two ways, both by grace. First, believers are already counted righteous in Christ: his obedience and death are credited to them, so no charge can stand (Romans 8:33–34). Second, God is making them holy in fact, a work begun at conversion and completed at Christ’s coming, when we shall be like him (1 John 3:2). The first is justification, the second sanctification, and Paul prays for the second on the basis of the first. You will stand blameless on that day not because you finally got it right, but because Christ did, and because the God who began the work will finish it (5:23–24).

How do I love people who make my life difficult? Ask God for it, as Paul does; it is his gift before it is your effort. Then do concrete good: pray for them specifically, speak well of them where you honestly can, refuse revenge, and look for a practical kindness. Love does not pretend the harm did not happen, nor require you to stay in danger or trust someone who has not changed. But it wishes them good, and leaves judgment to God.

Where Christians differ: coming for his saints, or with them? Some dispensationalists (Christians who read the Bible as a series of distinct eras and expect separate futures for Israel and the church) distinguish Christ coming for his saints (a secret rapture) from coming with his saints (seven years later). They hold it from careful study of prophecy and real longing for Christ’s appearing, and this commentary honours them as brothers. This commentary’s view: Paul describes one coming, at which Christ brings the souls of departed believers with him, raises their bodies, gathers the living, and judges the world (4:14–17; 2 Thessalonians 1:7–10). He comes both for and with his saints in a single, visible, glorious return. There is no secret rapture. Paul’s second letter adds that this one coming will be preceded by the rebellion and the revealing of the man of lawlessness (2 Thessalonians 2:1–3): it is near and certain, but it will not come unheralded.
