keyVerse.quote: and may the Lord make you increase and abound in love for one another and for all, as we do for you, so that he may establish your hearts blameless in holiness before our God and Father, at the coming of our Lord Jesus with all his saints.
keyVerse.note: The chapter’s anxiety, relief and joy end in this prayer, and it sets out the agenda for the rest of the letter: love (4:9–12), holiness (4:1–8; 5:23) and the coming of Jesus (4:13–5:11). Paul asks God to do in them what Timothy could only encourage, and he sets the whole Christian life within view of the day when Christ comes.

3.reflection:
Paul says believers are “destined for” affliction (v. 3), and that he told the Thessalonians so before it came (v. 4). How does knowing in advance that following Christ will cost something help you stand when it does? Where is the pressure on your faith more like a gentle coaxing than a battering ram?

Paul could not bear the silence, so he sent Timothy, and Timothy’s report brought him back to life (vv. 1–8). Who in your life might need someone to go to them, or a word of encouragement, this week? And whose faithfulness has strengthened you without their knowing it?

Paul speaks of “what is lacking” in the faith of a church he has just praised (v. 10). What gaps in your understanding or obedience would you like filled, and how might your group help one another grow?

Paul prays for love “for all”, including those making the church’s life hard, and for hearts blameless at Christ’s coming (vv. 12–13). Why do you think he asks God for these things before he commands them? How would praying this prayer for one another change your church?

4.title: Holy Living and the Blessed Hope
4.overview:
Where we are. The letter now turns from looking back to looking ahead. Paul begins to supply what was lacking in their faith (3:10), following the order of his prayer in 3:12–13: holiness, love, and the coming of the Lord Jesus.

The message. God’s will is that his people be made holy, in their bodies, their love and their daily work, as they wait for the Jesus who died and rose to come again. Believers who die are not lost or left behind: God will bring them with Jesus, the dead in Christ will rise first, and all his people together will be with the Lord for ever.

Why it was said. Most of the church had come straight from idols, from a world where a man’s use of slaves and prostitutes was unremarkable, manual work was despised, and the grave held no hope (see the introduction). Some were neglecting their work, and the deaths of believers had raised a fear Paul had had no time to answer: would those who died miss the Lord’s coming?

How the chapter makes its case. First, holiness in the body (vv. 1–8): God’s will is your sanctification, which means keeping clear of sexual immorality, governing your body in honour, and never wronging a brother, because the Lord avenges such wrongs and God gives you his Holy Spirit. Then love and work (vv. 9–12): God has taught them to love one another, so let it grow; and let them make it their ambition to live quietly and work with their hands. Last, hope in grief (vv. 13–18): Christians grieve, but not without hope, because Jesus died and rose; the Lord will descend, the dead in Christ will rise first, the living will be caught up with them, “and so we will always be with the Lord.”

Where it leads. The instructions come through the Lord Jesus (v. 2); the Spirit who makes bodies holy is the Spirit he poured out; and the whole hope of the Christian dead rests on one sentence: “Jesus died and rose again.” He took death in full, so that for those who belong to him it has become sleep. He will come in person, and the comfort at the end is not mainly a place but a person: we will “always be with the Lord.”

For us. God has told you his will plainly: be holy, love more, work quietly. Purity, kindness and an honest day’s work are the shape of a life lived for his pleasure while you wait. And at every Christian grave there are words to say to one another.

verseByVerse.ref: 4:1–8 – The Will of God Is Your Sanctification
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s will is that his people be made holy, and holiness begins in the body. Paul asks them to keep growing in the life that pleases God, as the Lord Jesus taught them (vv. 1–2). That will means keeping clear of sexual immorality, governing their own bodies in holiness and honour, unlike those who do not know God (vv. 3–5), and never wronging a brother, for the Lord avenges such wrongs (v. 6). God called them to holiness, so to dismiss this teaching is to dismiss God, who goes on giving them his Holy Spirit (vv. 7–8).
verseByVerse.theology:
The body, and who lives in it

Paul grounds Christian sexual ethics not in his own authority but in the Holy Spirit, whom God goes on giving (see the note on vv. 7–8).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: In the Greek and Roman world, sexual rules depended on rank and ownership (see the note on vv. 3–5).

Now: Verse 6 names the victim (see the note on v. 6).

verseByVerse.quote: Finally, then, brothers, we ask and urge you in the Lord Jesus, that as you received from us how you ought to walk and to please God, just as you are doing, that you do so more and more. For you know what instructions we gave you through the Lord Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul urges them to keep growing in the life that pleases God, following the instructions he gave them from the Lord Jesus.

Finally, then, brothers. Finally (loipon) does not mean Paul is winding up; it means “for the rest”, and marks the turn from report to request.

Ask and urge. A request and an appeal (parakaleō, to come alongside), not bare commands, though Paul had every right to issue them (2:6).

To please God. Paul’s aim is a person pleased, not a rulebook kept: you can satisfy a rule without thinking of its giver, but not please a person that way. The Lord Jesus always did what pleased his Father, and the Father said so from heaven; joined to him, sinners like us can please God too, not to earn his love but because we have it.

More and more. Before he asks for anything he confirms that they are doing it already. More and more comes twice (vv. 1, 10): the Christian life is growth, not maintenance, and doing well is the ground for going further. A way of encouragement worth copying: name what is good honestly, then call for growth.

Instructions through the Lord Jesus. Instructions (parangelia) are orders passed down from a superior, and they were never Paul’s: they came through him from the Lord Jesus, and he was as much under them as they were. The risen Christ sent his apostles to make disciples, “teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you” (Matthew 28:20). And his commands come from the one who loved us first, which is why they are not burdensome (1 John 5:3).

If I fail, is God displeased with me as his child? In Christ you are accepted completely and permanently; your standing rests on Christ’s obedience, not yours, and your failures do not undo your adoption (Romans 8:1, 15). But a loving Father can be grieved by what his children do and glad when they obey, and Scripture speaks of both (Ephesians 4:30; Colossians 1:10). So you live from acceptance, not for it, and you can actually bring God pleasure, one of the most astonishing things the Bible says about ordinary believers.

verseByVerse.quote: For this is the will of God, your sanctification: that you abstain from sexual immorality; that each one of you know how to control his own body in holiness and honor, not in the passion of lust like the Gentiles who do not know God;
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s will for every believer is that they be made holy, and that includes keeping clear of all sexual sin and governing their bodies in honour, not in the lust of those who do not know God.

Your sanctification. People often wish they knew God’s will for their lives. Here it is in a sentence, and it is not about a job, a marriage or a city: your sanctification (hagiasmos), being made holy. Whatever else God leaves undisclosed, this he has told us plainly.

Abstain from sexual immorality. Abstain (apechomai) means keep your distance. Sexual immorality (porneia) is the broad word covering every sexual act outside the marriage of a man and a woman, the union Jesus grounds in the creation of male and female (Genesis 2:24; Matthew 19:4–6).

Control his own body. The ESV takes Paul to mean self-control (on the other possible reading, see the box below). Either way, sexual life is to be lived in holiness and honour, which rules out using another person as a tool for one’s own appetite.

Like the Gentiles who do not know God. Paul draws a straight line from not knowing God to desire out of control (pathos epithymias, the passion of craving). Not that pagans were uniquely wicked; the ancient world had moralists who taught restraint. But where God is not known, there is no reason to treat the body as anything but a means of pleasure. Those who know God have both a reason and a power to be pure.

The world it landed in. A married man’s use of slaves, prostitutes and concubines was unremarkable; another citizen’s wife was forbidden, because that was theft from him. A speech preserved under Demosthenes’ name could set out the arrangement without embarrassment: courtesans for pleasure, concubines for daily care, wives for legitimate children. Into that world Paul brings one standard for men and women alike.

By that will. Before God’s will for our holiness was a command to us, it was a task his Son came to carry out: “by that will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all” (Hebrews 10:10). Believers have already been set apart as God’s own by Christ’s body given on the cross; now, in their own bodies, they are being made holy in fact. You are not trying to become God’s by keeping pure; you are his already, and purity is learning to live as what you are.

What it does not mean. Not that sex itself is unholy. Within marriage it is God’s good gift (1 Corinthians 7:3–5; Hebrews 13:4). Sexual desire must be governed by holiness.

In everyday life. Identify where your purity is most tested, a device, a time of night, a relationship, a habit of thought, and make one concrete change there today: move the phone, install accountability, end the conversation, tell a trusted believer. Purity seldom comes as heroic resistance in the moment; usually it comes through wise decisions made beforehand.

Does sexual immorality include things like pornography or living together before marriage? Yes. Jesus took the standard into the heart: looking with lustful intent is adultery there (Matthew 5:28). Pornography trains the heart in exactly the lust Paul describes and uses real people as instruments. Living together as though married takes the gift without the covenant. The call is not to shame but to holiness: get out of the situation, bring it into the light with a trusted believer, and take the practical steps that make purity possible.

I have already sinned sexually. Can I be made clean? Yes, completely. Paul lists the sexually immoral among those who will not inherit the kingdom, and then says: such were some of you, but you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God (1 Corinthians 6:9–11). Christ’s blood cleanses every sin confessed to him (1 John 1:9). You may live with consequences and need help to break patterns, but you are not second-class: in Christ you are clean, and holiness from here on is possible.

What about desires I did not choose? Being tempted is not sinning; the Lord Jesus felt the full pressure of temptation and never gave way (Hebrews 4:15). Many Christians carry desires they did not choose, whether for sex outside marriage, for the same sex, or simply strong desire with no spouse. The call to each is the same: do not feed the desire, do not act on it, bring it honestly to God, and find support in the church. Singleness lived in purity is no lesser life; the Lord Jesus lived it.

Uncertain wording. Verse 4 contains a genuine translation question, as the ESV footnote notes. The word is skeuos, vessel, used of the body (2 Corinthians 4:7) and of a wife (1 Peter 3:7), and the verb can mean to gain or acquire as well as to control. So Paul may mean know how to control his own body, or know how to take a wife for himself in holiness and honour. Both readings are old and defensible. The ESV’s reading, body, is the more likely: the context is self-control, and the command is given to each one of you, single and married.
verseByVerse.note: To “control his own body” may instead mean “take a wife for himself”; the phrase can be read either way.

verseByVerse.quote: that no one transgress and wrong his brother in this matter, because the Lord is an avenger in all these things, as we told you beforehand and solemnly warned you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sexual sin always wrongs a real person, and the Lord himself will bring justice for those wronged.

Transgress and wrong his brother. Transgress (hyperbainō) means to overstep a boundary. Wrong (pleonekteō) means to overreach, to take advantage, to defraud, a word at home in business dealings: taking what was not yours to get more for yourself.

Sexual sin is never private. Our culture treats sex between consenting adults as private. Paul sees a brother or sister on the other side of it: the person used, the spouse betrayed, the family fractured, the future spouse defrauded. It is theft from someone Christ died for.

An avenger. An avenger (ekdikos) brings justice for the wronged (compare Hebrews 13:4). Sexual sin often goes unpunished in this life, and the powerful have generally used people and kept their reputation; but there is a court that does not work that way. To the person who has been wronged and never received justice, this verse is not a threat but a promise.

Told you beforehand. Sexual ethics was part of the basic instruction for new converts, not a stricter rule added later.

The Lord who avenges. Most likely the Lord Jesus, whom Paul’s next letter shows revealed from heaven in flaming fire, inflicting vengeance on those who do not know God (2 Thessalonians 1:7–8), the phrase just used of the pagans (4:5). The one who will right every sexual wrong took children in his arms and blessed them, and said it would be better to be drowned with a millstone round the neck than to cause a little one to stumble (Mark 10:16; Matthew 18:6). His tenderness toward the vulnerable and his anger at those who use them are the same love.

The avenger is also the Saviour. The avenger is good news for every victim the world forgot. And the same Lord bore the punishment of every sinner who flees to him, so he is also the Saviour of the wrongdoer who repents. That is why Paul warns: there is a way out. Confess, turn, make what restitution can be made, and run to Christ. He is the God who sees (Genesis 16:13).

I was the one wronged. What does this verse say to me? God is on your side. What was done to you was a real wrong, an overstepping and a theft, and God takes it personally. If you were abused, it was never your fault, and the church must never hide or tolerate it: report it to the authorities, seek safety, and find people who will care for you. His promise to avenge means you need not carry the burden of making it right yourself. He will judge justly, and in Christ he can also heal what was broken.

verseByVerse.quote: For God has not called us for impurity, but in holiness. Therefore whoever disregards this, disregards not man but God, who gives his Holy Spirit to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God called his people into holiness, so whoever rejects this teaching rejects God himself, who keeps giving them his Holy Spirit.

Called in holiness. Paul argues not from consequences but from what they were summoned into (1 Peter 1:15–16). Holiness is not an advanced option for keen Christians; it is what God called us to.

Not man but God. To disregard (atheteō) is to set aside as having no authority. The instruction was never Paul’s (v. 2), so whoever sets it aside is dealing not with Paul but with God.

Who gives his Holy Spirit. Here is the reason beneath the whole paragraph. The tense is continuous, “who goes on giving”, and the Greek says literally “into you”. So the argument for sexual holiness ends not with a threat but with a Person, continually given, living in the very body under discussion. Your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit, and you were bought with a price (1 Corinthians 6:19–20). The reason is not that God is restrictive but that he has moved in, and that the Holy One should dwell in such houses is the wonder of the gospel. Sexual sin grieves him, and he gives the power to be holy.

Poured out by the exalted Son. The Spirit God gives is the Spirit of Christ (Romans 8:9), poured out by the risen and exalted Jesus (Acts 2:33). The Spirit inside a believer’s body is the fruit of Christ’s cross and ascension, and he aims to make us like Christ: we “are being transformed into the same image” (2 Corinthians 3:18). The holiness Paul asks for is Christ’s likeness, formed by Christ’s Spirit.

Was this not just Paul’s culture? Our culture has moved on. The culture of Paul’s day was far more permissive than his teaching, so this was never his culture talking; it was the gospel confronting it, with the Lord Jesus’ authority. Cultures change, but the God who made our bodies and the Spirit who lives in them do not. What feels old-fashioned in one century is often what the next discovers it needed.

If the Spirit lives in me, why do I still struggle with lust? Because the Spirit’s coming starts a war rather than ending one at once. The flesh, our old sinful nature, desires against the Spirit (Galatians 5:17), and every believer fights until glory. The struggle itself is a sign of his presence. Keep fighting by the means he gives: Scripture, prayer, confession, accountability, fleeing temptation, and filling your life with better things. He who gives his Spirit continually will not abandon the fight in you.

Textual note. Some manuscripts, followed by the KJV, read “who has given”; the present “who gives” is better supported, and most modern Bibles follow it.

verseByVerse.ref: 4:9–12 – Brotherly Love and the Quiet Life
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Love for the family of God and honest, quiet work belong together. God himself has taught them to love one another, and they already love believers across Macedonia, yet they are to do so more and more (vv. 9–10). Love also means ambition for a quiet life: minding their own affairs and working with their hands, so that outsiders respect them and they are a burden to no one (vv. 11–12).
verseByVerse.theology:
The new covenant, arrived

In calling them “taught by God”, Paul reaches for Jeremiah’s new covenant promise that God would write his law on their hearts (see the note on vv. 9–10).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Why some may have stopped working is discussed at vv. 11–12.

Now: Expecting the Lord’s return should make a Christian more reliable, not less (see the note on vv. 11–12).

verseByVerse.quote: Now concerning brotherly love you have no need for anyone to write to you, for you yourselves have been taught by God to love one another, for that indeed is what you are doing to all the brothers throughout Macedonia. But we urge you, brothers, to do this more and more,
verseByVerse.commentary:
God himself has taught them to love one another, and they already do so across Macedonia, but Paul urges them to love more and more.

Now concerning brotherly love. Paul turns to philadelphia, love for fellow believers as family. You have no need for anyone to write to you, he says, and then writes anyway: a gracious way of raising a subject they know. “Now concerning” (peri de) introduces the church’s own questions in 1 Corinthians (7:1, 25; 8:1); here and at 4:13 and 5:1 it probably marks questions Timothy brought back, which is why the rest of the letter reads like a set of answers.

Taught by God. God-taught (theodidaktoi) appears in no earlier surviving Greek. Paul is almost certainly reaching for Jeremiah’s promise of a new covenant, in which God himself would teach his people from within: “I will write it on their hearts … they shall all know me” (Jeremiah 31:33–34; John 6:45). The promised covenant had arrived among former pagans a few months old, not through excellent teaching, since Paul had only weeks, but because God had written it inside them.

Throughout Macedonia. The love had travelled beyond their congregation, perhaps through hospitality and gifts for the needy: a young, poor, persecuted church already answering Paul’s prayer (3:12).

The new covenant in his blood. The promised covenant was not established by a lecture. Jesus took the cup and said, this cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood (Luke 22:20). God-taught love was learned at that table and that cross: “just as I have loved you, you also are to love one another” (John 13:34).

Not ashamed to call them brothers. Many had lost their families when they turned from the household gods, and God gave them brothers and sisters across a province. The Son of God is not ashamed to call such people his brothers (Hebrews 2:11), and a family bought with blood is the one family no persecution can break up.

How can I love a fellow believer I find difficult? God taught you to love, not to like; affection may follow, but love begins with will and action. Pray for them; it is hard to keep resenting someone you pray for. Look for Christ in them, and do them good in small, concrete ways. Overlook what can be overlooked, and speak honestly and gently about what cannot (Matthew 18:15). And remember that someone in your church is probably finding you difficult too.

What does loving believers in other churches look like? What the Thessalonians did: hospitality, prayer, practical help. Pray by name for other gospel churches in your town, welcome visiting believers, give to churches in need, and speak well of other faithful congregations rather than competing with them.

verseByVerse.quote: and to aspire to live quietly, and to mind your own affairs, and to work with your hands, as we instructed you, so that you may walk properly before outsiders and be dependent on no one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Make it your ambition to live a quiet, ordinary, hard-working life, so that outsiders respect the gospel and you burden no one.

Aspire to live quietly. Almost a joke in Greek: philotimeomai, to be ambitious, the word for competing for public distinction, joined to hēsychazō, to be quiet. Make it your ambition to be unremarkable.

Mind your own affairs. The natural companion: attend to your own business rather than everyone else’s (2 Thessalonians 3:11).

Work with your hands. This offended Greek pride: manual labour was for slaves and the poor. Paul, who had done it among them night and day (2:9), tells them to do it too. The Lord of glory spent most of his years in a quiet town working with his hands, and the Father was well pleased with him before he had preached a sermon. He has hallowed the ordinary day and the honest trade.

Why this needed saying. Perhaps partly because of the hope Paul turns to next: if the Lord is returning soon, why keep working? Paul does not say so, and we cannot be sure. The problem grew worse; in the second letter he says, “If anyone is not willing to work, let him not eat” (2 Thessalonians 3:6–12). Expecting the Lord should make you more reliable, not less; and idleness is a failure of love, since the idle man’s food comes from his brothers.

Properly before outsiders. Properly (euschēmonōs) means decently, and the city was watching (1:8): an honest, working, calm church is an argument for the gospel. Being dependent on no one does not reject Christian generosity; it refuses to become a weight on people needlessly.

Found at work when he comes. The Lord Jesus had already drawn the connection: “Blessed is that servant whom his master will find so doing when he comes” (Luke 12:43). The best way to be ready for him is to be found at the bench, the desk or the sink, doing the ordinary work for him.

The ambition that never arrives. Paul’s phrase cuts across a culture that runs on striving. Adam Smith, no enemy of ambition, wrote in The Theory of Moral Sentiments about “the poor man’s son, whom heaven in its anger has visited with ambition”. He spends his life pursuing a greatness he imagines will finally let him rest, and in old age finds that the ease he chased was within reach all along. Most of us are that son in some form: the next role, the next house, the next proof that we count, each promising a quiet it never delivers. Church can feed the same hunger. We are working for a verdict, and the work never ends. The gospel gives the verdict first: “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28). Then at last we can be ambitious in Paul’s sense: to do good work well, for others, without needing it to make us somebody.

In everyday life. The New Testament’s ambition for most Christians is not a platform but ordinary competence: your work done well, your business minded, nobody poorer for having you around. Do today’s work for the Lord, and leave one piece of other people’s business alone.

Does “live quietly” mean Christians should stay out of public life? No. Paul does not forbid Christians to hold office, vote, speak for justice or serve their city; he used his own citizenship and appealed to Caesar. He forbids restlessness, meddling and agitation: the busybody who manages everyone’s business but his own. A Christian may serve in public life, with a quiet spirit, not seeking to be noticed.

What if I cannot work, or cannot find work? Then this verse is not a rebuke to you. Paul’s target is those who can work and will not. The sick, the elderly, the disabled, those caring for others, and those looking for work and not finding it are to be cared for by the church gladly (1 Timothy 5:3–16; Galatians 6:10). Do what you can, receive help without shame, and remember that your worth to God was never measured by wages.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Christians grieve, but not without hope, because Jesus died and rose again. Paul writes so that the church will not grieve like those who have no hope (v. 13): God will bring with Jesus those who have died (v. 14). By a word from the Lord, the living will have no advantage; the Lord himself will descend, the dead in Christ will rise first (vv. 15–16), and the living will be caught up with them to meet him, and so be with him for ever (v. 17). These are words to comfort one another with (v. 18).
verseByVerse.theology:
The meeting on the road

“To meet the Lord” (v. 17) is the language of a city’s delegation going out along the road to greet an arriving king and escort him in (Acts 28:15). The passage describes one loud, public, personal arrival, and it gives no timetable.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: On how a Christian funeral looked against the tomb inscriptions of that world, see the note on v. 13.

Now: Paul does not forbid grief, only grief without hope (v. 13); and the passage is for comforting one another at gravesides (v. 18), not for building charts.

verseByVerse.quote: But we do not want you to be uninformed, brothers, about those who are asleep, that you may not grieve as others do who have no hope.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul tells them the truth about believers who have died, so that their grief, though real, will be full of hope.

Not uninformed. Here is the pastoral emergency behind the letter. Some in the church had died, and in a few weeks Paul had not covered what happens to a believer who dies before the Lord arrives. Would they miss it? His answer to grief is information: not “feel differently” or “pray harder”, but a fact they did not know. Sometimes the comfort the grieving most need is the truth.

Those who are asleep. To fall asleep (koimaomai) is the New Testament’s usual word for the death of a believer (Acts 7:60; 1 Corinthians 15:18); our word cemetery comes from the same root, a sleeping place. The picture says death is temporary and there will be a waking. It is not a soft way of avoiding death; it is the Lord’s own word: “Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep, but I go to awaken him” (John 11:11). Christians call their dead asleep because Jesus did, and because he proved it at a tomb.

Not as others do. Paul does not forbid grief (lypeō): Christians grieve, but not like people with nothing ahead. To make bereaved believers feel that tears are a failure of faith is a cruelty this verse does not support. Jesus wept at a grave he was about to open (John 11:35). What Christian hope changes is not whether you weep but what you know while you are weeping.

Who have no hope. This was simply accurate. One Latin formula, common enough to be abbreviated on gravestones, ran, “I was not, I was, I am not, I care not.” A common consolation was that nobody ever comes back, so grieve and be done. Christian funerals in Thessalonica must have looked extraordinary: the same tears, and something else entirely.

Not a pit but a bed. For his people the grave is not a pit but a bed, and morning is coming, because the one who will wake them went down into the darkest night himself and came back at dawn. Death is only sleep when the one who speaks over it is the resurrection and the life (John 11:25). The gravestones of that world said, “I care not.” Heaven’s answer is a Saviour who knows each of his sleeping friends by name.

How long is it right to grieve? Christian hope sets no deadline for tears; it gives firm ground to stand on while you weep. Grief that stops you functioning is a sign to seek help, not a lack of faith.

What about loved ones who died without faith in Christ? The hardest grief. Paul’s comfort here is for those who die in Christ, and Scripture offers no hope of salvation apart from him; we must not invent one. But we do not know what passed between a person and God in their last hours; the thief on the cross was saved at the very end. So we neither pronounce on them nor pretend. We leave them to the Judge of all the earth, who will do right, grieve honestly, and speak of Christ to the living while there is time.

Where Christians differ: soul sleep. Some sincere Christians take asleep to mean that the souls of the dead are unconscious until the resurrection. This commentary’s view: Sleep describes the body’s rest and the certainty of waking. The souls of believers are immediately with Christ, consciously and joyfully (Philippians 1:23; 2 Corinthians 5:8; Luke 23:43). God will bring them with Jesus (v. 14): they are with him now. Their bodies sleep until the resurrection, as the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession teach (Westminster 32.1; 1689 31.1).
verseByVerse.note: “Asleep” was a common Christian way of speaking of believers who had died.

verseByVerse.quote: For since we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so, through Jesus, God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because Jesus died and rose again, God will bring with him those who have died believing in him.

Jesus died and rose again. The argument is one sentence long and rests on a historical event: not a theory about the soul, but the empty tomb.

Joined to him, not merely like him. Believers are in him, and what happened to the head happens to the body: Christ the firstfruits, then at his coming those who belong to him (1 Corinthians 15:20–23). Firstfruits are the first sheaf cut: not a hopeful sign that a harvest might follow, but the beginning of the harvest itself.

Died, and fallen asleep. Of Jesus Paul says died; of believers, fallen asleep. He will not soften the cross: Jesus died in the full and terrible sense, bearing death’s curse, and because he took death in full it has become sleep for all who belong to him.

God will bring with him. The dead are not left behind: when Jesus comes, they come with him, for their souls are already with Christ, to be reunited with their raised bodies. They feared their dead had missed the appointment; they will be in the procession, not as latecomers admitted at the back, but coming with the King.

Is this not just wishful thinking, a story people tell to cope with death? Wishful thinking produces vague hopes, that the dead live on in our memories or the stars. Paul’s hope rests on a public claim about a particular tomb, made within twenty years, when hundreds of witnesses could still be questioned (1 Corinthians 15:6). And the first Christians were Jews, most of whom expected the righteous to rise together at the end of history, not one man in the middle of it; people do not easily invent a hope that cuts across everything they expected. The witnesses said they had seen him, and many suffered for saying so. If he did not rise, Christians are to be pitied (1 Corinthians 15:17–19); if he did, death is not the end of anyone who belongs to him.

Why does the resurrection of the body matter, if the soul is already with Christ? Because God made us body and soul, and salvation rescues the whole person. Being with Christ now is far better (Philippians 1:23), but it is not the end: death tears apart what God joined, and the resurrection puts it back together, glorified. Christian hope is not escape from the body but the redemption of the body (Romans 8:23), in a renewed creation.

Does it matter what happens to the body: burial, cremation, lost at sea? God can raise any body, however it was lost; the martyrs burned and the sailors drowned are not beyond his reach (Revelation 20:13). Many Christians prefer burial, which pictures the body sown in hope, as the Lord’s was laid in a tomb; others choose cremation for good reasons, and it affects no one’s resurrection. Whatever is done, treat the body with honour: it belonged to someone God loves and will one day stand again.

Uncertain wording. “Through Jesus” can be read with “those who have fallen asleep” (those who died through, that is in, Jesus) or with “will bring” (God will bring them through Jesus). The Greek allows both, and translations differ. Either way, everything about a Christian’s death and future runs through the same person.

verseByVerse.quote: For this we declare to you by a word from the Lord, that we who are alive, who are left until the coming of the Lord, will not precede those who have fallen asleep. For the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a cry of command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the sound of the trumpet of God. And the dead in Christ will rise first.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the Lord’s own authority, Paul assures them that the living will have no advantage over the dead: the Lord himself will come from heaven, and the dead in Christ will rise first.

A word from the Lord. What follows is revelation, not Paul’s inference; he is careful about this distinction (1 Corinthians 7:10, 12). On what the word may have been, see the box below.

Will not precede. Precede (phthanō) means to get ahead of. They feared the dead had been left at the back of the queue; Paul says there is no queue.

The Lord himself. Not an angel sent to fetch them, but this same Jesus who was taken up, coming in person (1:10; Acts 1:11), his arrival announced by three sounds.

With a cry of command. A cry of command (keleusma) is the shout of an officer to troops: a word of authority. Perhaps it is the voice that raises the dead (John 5:28–29). He who once lay in a tomb will empty every tomb that holds his own.

With the voice of an archangel. A chief angel, perhaps Michael (Jude 9): the angels who announced his birth and resurrection will herald his return.

The trumpet of God. This is the last trumpet (1 Corinthians 15:52; Matthew 24:31). In Israel’s Scriptures the trumpet summoned the assembly and announced God’s presence (Exodus 19:16). Whatever else the passage describes, it does not describe anything secret.

The dead in Christ will rise first. The answer, stated flatly, and “in Christ” carries the weight. They died in union with him, and death did not break that union; it only hid it. By faith and the Spirit believers are so joined to him that what is his becomes theirs: his death for sin, his new life, and one day his resurrection (Romans 6:5). Paul is answering one grieving congregation about their own dead, not giving a general account of the resurrection; all will be raised in the end (John 5:28–29; Acts 24:15).

Did Paul expect to be alive when Christ returned? He writes “we who are alive” because he identifies himself with whoever will be living then; he did not know when it would be (5:1–2), and later he expects to die (2 Timothy 4:6). Some readers think he hoped at this stage to live to see it; even so, he never taught a date, and nothing he affirmed has failed. He was not mistaken; he was ready, as every generation should be.

Is Jesus the archangel? Jehovah’s Witnesses identify him with Michael. No: the Lord descends with an archangel’s voice as with the trumpet; the archangel accompanies him. Hebrews says God never called any angel his Son (Hebrews 1:5), and that all God’s angels worship him (Hebrews 1:6).

What body will the dead in Christ rise with? Your own body, recognisably you, but transformed: imperishable, glorious, powerful, fitted for the life of the Spirit (1 Corinthians 15:42–44). The risen Jesus is the pattern: touchable, eating, bearing his wounds, yet no longer subject to death. Our lowly bodies will be made like his glorious body (Philippians 3:21): no more illness, ageing or disability, and no more sin in our members. And those still alive when he comes will be changed in a moment, so that the risen and the living meet him in the same glory (1 Corinthians 15:51–52).

Uncertain wording. We do not know exactly what the “word from the Lord” was: a saying of Jesus not recorded in the Gospels, a direct revelation to Paul or another prophet, or a summary of Jesus’ teaching such as Matthew 24:30–31. Its source and authority are clear.

verseByVerse.quote: Then we who are alive, who are left, will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so we will always be with the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Living believers will be caught up together with the risen dead to meet the Lord as he comes, and from then on they will always be with him.

Caught up together with them. Caught up (harpazō) means seized or snatched, as when the Spirit carried Philip away (Acts 8:39). In Latin it became rapiemur, which is where the English word rapture comes from. So the word is biblical; the question is what the scene describes. Together with them: the separation of death undone in an instant. In the clouds: often the sign of God’s presence (Exodus 19:9; Acts 1:9; Daniel 7:13).

To meet the Lord in the air. To meet (eis apantēsin) is almost a set phrase for a formal welcome. When a king approached a city, the citizens went out along the road to greet him and then escorted him in. The word is used of the virgins going out to meet the bridegroom (Matthew 25:6), and of the Roman Christians who walked down the Appian Way to meet Paul (Acts 28:15).

The King comes home. Paul has used parousia, the word for a royal visit, since 2:19. Read like this, the passage is not about the church being removed from the earth but about the King coming to it: he arrives, his people, the dead first and then the living, go out to meet him, and the procession comes home. Paul does not describe what follows the meeting, so the picture is a pointer rather than a proof; but it fits the rest of Scripture, where the King comes to stay.

Always with the Lord. Here Paul’s emphasis falls: the air is merely where the meeting happens; the comfort is the permanence. What the Thessalonians were frightened of losing, the presence of Christ and of each other, turns out to be the one thing that cannot now be interrupted. The heart of the hope is not mainly a place, but a person.

Does this mean I should be afraid of being left behind? No. Popular stories of Christians vanishing while others are left to cope have taught many believers to fear, but there will be no secret disappearance. When Christ comes, every believer, living and dead, will be gathered to him, all at once and in plain sight. If you belong to Christ, you cannot be left behind. The fear this passage should remove is the fear of being forgotten.

Where will we live forever: in the air, in heaven? With the Lord, wherever he is, and Scripture shows where: a new heaven and a new earth, where the dwelling place of God is with man (Revelation 21:1–3; 2 Peter 3:13). Those who die now go to be with Christ in heaven, but the air is only the meeting place; the new earth is the home.

What about those who are alive when he comes: will they die? No. We shall not all sleep, Paul tells the Corinthians, but we shall all be changed, in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet (1 Corinthians 15:51–52). Believers alive at his coming will be transformed without passing through death. Raised or changed, the end is the same: always with the Lord.

Where Christians differ: the rapture. Many dispensationalists (Christians who read the Bible as a series of distinct eras, with separate futures for Israel and the church) teach a secret, pre-tribulation rapture: Christ will come invisibly to take believers to heaven, leaving the world to a seven-year tribulation, before returning visibly with them. Its holders are often among the most earnest students of prophecy and the most eager for Christ’s appearing, and they draw on real texts: God has not destined us for wrath (5:9), and believers are to be always ready. Faithful Christians differ here, and the difference does not touch the gospel. This commentary’s view: This passage describes the loudest, most public event imaginable: a shout, an archangel’s voice, God’s trumpet. The word meet describes going out to welcome a coming king and escort him back, which points to Christ’s coming to earth, not a removal to heaven. The same events (trumpet, gathering of the elect, coming on the clouds) describe Christ’s one visible return in Matthew 24:30–31. Scripture teaches one return of Christ, at the end of the age, when the dead are raised, the living changed and caught up, and all are judged (2 Thessalonians 1:7–10). The rapture is real, but it is part of that one glorious coming, not a separate secret event. This commentary’s wider view is amillennial: the thousand years of Revelation 20 picture Christ’s present reign between his first and second comings, not a later earthly kingdom, so his one return brings the end. That return is near, yet Paul tells this same church that it will be preceded by named events, the rebellion and the revealing of the man of lawlessness (2 Thessalonians 2:3).
verseByVerse.note: “Meet” was the word used of citizens going out to welcome an arriving dignitary and escort him into the city.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore encourage one another with these words.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This hope is given to be used: believers are to comfort and strengthen one another with these very words.

Encourage one another. The word means both to comfort and to exhort. Paul does not say: therefore construct a chart, or divide from those who read it differently. This was given to a bereaved congregation to be used on each other: not by Paul, far away, nor by the leaders only, but by ordinary believers comforting one another with doctrine. Our handling of it should be measured by that.

With these words. Paul expects the actual words to be repeated, at the graveside and to the widow when everyone else has gone back to normal; read at Christian funerals for nearly two thousand years, they have been.

The comfort has a name. Almost every sentence names Jesus: Jesus died and rose; God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep; the Lord himself will descend; we will always be with the Lord. Take his name out and nothing comforting is left. Simeon waited for the consolation (the comfort) of Israel and found it in the baby in his arms (Luke 2:25–32). The God of all comfort has given words that can be spoken over every Christian grave, and a day is coming when even these will not be needed: he will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more (Revelation 21:4).

What do I actually say to a grieving friend? Usually less, and later, than you think. In the first days, presence matters more than words: come, sit, bring food, weep with them (Romans 12:15). Do not explain the loss or hurry them toward feeling better. When the time is right, and especially if the one who died was a believer, say the truth simply: they are with the Lord, and you will see them again; Jesus died and rose, and he will bring them with him. Read these verses together. And keep coming back weeks and months later, when others have stopped.
