keyVerse.quote: For since we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so, through Jesus, God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep.
keyVerse.note: The whole Christian answer to death rests on this one sentence. Paul does not offer a theory about the soul but a fact about a tomb: because Jesus died and rose, those joined to him will rise and come with him. It is also what makes the rest of the chapter make sense, for those who expect to be with the Lord for ever have every reason to live for his pleasure now.

4.reflection:
Paul says plainly that “this is the will of God, your sanctification” (v. 3). How does it change your search for God’s will to know that this much is certain? Where in your daily life is that will most tested?

Verse 6 insists that sexual sin always wrongs a real person, and that the Lord avenges such wrongs. Why does our culture find this hard to accept, and how can a church be a place of both holiness and healing, for those who have done wrong and for those who have been wronged?

Paul tells an anxious, hopeful church to make it their ambition to live quietly, mind their own affairs and work with their hands (v. 11). What would that ambition look like in your work, your home and your online life?

Paul does not forbid grief but grief without hope (v. 13). How has Christian hope, or its absence, shaped grief you have known? What would it look like to “encourage one another with these words” (v. 18) in your church this year?

5.title: Children of the Day
5.overview:
Where we are. Having answered what happens to believers who die (4:13–18), Paul takes up the question that naturally follows, “When?”, and then closes the letter with the life of a waiting church and a last prayer.

The message. No one can know when the day of the Lord will come, and no one needs to. It will fall like a thief on a world that feels secure, but it cannot ambush those who belong to Christ, because God has appointed them not to wrath but to salvation through the Jesus who died for them. So live awake: armed with faith, love and hope, caring for one another, rejoicing, praying and giving thanks, and trusting the faithful God who will finish making you holy.

Why it was said. A church that had just buried friends, and was suffering for its faith (see the introduction), could easily swing between feverish guessing about dates and dread at the talk of wrath. Paul refuses to give a date, as Jesus did, and gives them instead a certainty and a way to live. Its young leaders also needed backing, and its members needed to know how to deal with the idle, the frightened and the weak among them.

How the chapter makes its case. First, children of the day (vv. 1–11): the day comes suddenly on those saying “peace and security” (vv. 1–3); but believers are children of light (vv. 4–5), so they stay awake and sober, dressed in faith, love and hope (vv. 6–8), because God has destined them for salvation through Christ who died for them (vv. 9–10); so they encourage one another (v. 11). Then life together (vv. 12–22): honour those who lead, keep the peace, give each struggling member what he needs, never take revenge, rejoice, pray and give thanks, and test everything said in God’s name. Last, kept blameless (vv. 23–28): the commands are wrapped in prayer and a promise, “He who calls you is faithful; he will surely do it,” and the letter ends with grace.

Where it leads. The day of the Lord, which the prophets dreaded, now has a face: it is the day of the Jesus who “died for us so that whether we are awake or asleep we might live with him” (v. 10). The wrath that day brings has already fallen on him, so his people can wait for it without terror. Even the armour they wear was first his (Isaiah 59:17), and the holiness he asks of them he will himself complete.

For us. Do not try to work out the date; be ready every day. Ask whether you are awake or drifting, who in your church needs warning, comfort or a steady arm, and rest the outcome on the faithful God, not on your own staying power.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Believers cannot know when Christ will return, but they need not fear it, because they belong to the day. The day of the Lord will come like a thief, bringing sudden ruin on a world that thinks itself secure (vv. 1–3). But the children of light will not be ambushed (vv. 4–5), so they stay awake and sober, clothed in faith, love and hope (vv. 6–8). Beneath it all lies God’s appointment: not wrath, but salvation through Christ who died for them, so that alive or dead they will live with him (vv. 9–10). That is the truth they are to speak to one another (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology:
Not destined for wrath

God’s purpose for his people was settled in advance, and settled on salvation rather than wrath (v. 9), not because of their performance but because the Lord Jesus “died for us” (v. 10).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: “Peace and security” was close to an imperial slogan (see the note on v. 3).

Now: Paul tells them what they are, children of the day, before he tells them to stay awake (vv. 5–6). Tell people to stay awake in order to become God’s children, and you get exhausted Christians.

verseByVerse.quote: Now concerning the times and the seasons, brothers, you have no need to have anything written to you. For you yourselves are fully aware that the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one can know when the day of the Lord will come, and no one needs to: it is certain, and it will come without warning.

Times and seasons. After what happens to their dead (4:13–18) comes the next question: when? Paul politely declines to answer. The two Greek words, chronos and kairos, together mean simply “when”, and Jesus used the same pair: “It is not for you to know times or seasons that the Father has fixed by his own authority” (Acts 1:7). Their future was not in a calendar but in a Person.

Like a thief. The image comes from Jesus himself (Matthew 24:43; Revelation 16:15). A thief gives no warning, so working out the date is not merely difficult; it contradicts the teaching.

The day has a face. “The day of the LORD” is the prophets’ name for the day God comes to judge: “darkness, and not light” for people who assumed it would be good news for them (Amos 5:18–20; Joel 2:31). Paul uses that name, without explanation, for the day Jesus returns, and so the day now has a face: the Jesus they already know, who came once to die for them (v. 10). For the secure world the day is ruin; for those in Christ it is the arrival of their Saviour, because the judgment the prophets warned of has already fallen on him at the cross. He comes like a thief to the sleeping world, but as a bridegroom to his waiting bride. That is why Paul can leave the date unknown and the church unafraid.

What it does not mean. Not that the day will be secret. It will be sudden, but visible to all.

Then why do so many people try to work out the date? Because uncertainty is uncomfortable, and a date feels like control. But every attempt has failed, and some have done real harm: believers sold homes, quit jobs or lost faith when the date passed. Even the angels do not know (Matthew 24:36). If someone claims to have found the date, or says it must fall within so many years, kindly set it aside: the Lord has told us everything we need, and he has not told us that. The right response to not knowing when is to be ready always.

After nearly two thousand years, was the early church simply wrong? Paul taught not a date but that no date can be known, and no New Testament writer sets one. The hardest sayings are those such as “this generation will not pass away until all these things take place” (Matthew 24:34). Many careful readers take them to refer to the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70, which did come within that generation; such texts need care, but they do not set a date for the end. The last days began when Christ came (Hebrews 1:2), so his return is the next great act in God’s plan, and that is what “near” means. As for the delay: with the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and he is not slow but patient, not wishing that any should perish but that all should reach repentance (2 Peter 3:8–9). Every year he waits is another year of mercy to a world that does not deserve it.

Should the signs in the news make me think the end is very near? The end may be near; it has been near, in the biblical sense, since the ascension (Romans 13:11–12; James 5:8). Wars and earthquakes, Jesus said, are the beginning of the birth pains, not the end (Matthew 24:6–8), and they have marked every age. Read the news as a reminder that this world is passing, not as a code to crack; Paul’s second letter adds that the rebellion and the man of lawlessness come first (2 Thessalonians 2:3), so date-setters need not panic anyone. Live each day ready to meet him, and plan your life as though he might not come for a hundred years. Both are faithful.

verseByVerse.quote: While people are saying, "There is peace and security," then sudden destruction will come upon them as labor pains come upon a pregnant woman, and they will not escape.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The day will fall without warning on a world that feels most secure, and those who are not ready will not escape it.

Peace and security. The pax Romana (the Roman peace) was the empire’s proudest claim, peace and safety guaranteed by the legions, and Thessalonica had prospered under it (see the introduction). So had Jerusalem, when its false prophets kept saying “Peace, peace” when there was no peace (Jeremiah 6:14). Ruin comes just as people repeat the slogan: a civilisation sure it will last for ever is the least prepared of all.

Sudden destruction. Destruction (olethros) is ruin: not ceasing to exist but eternal loss, being shut out from the presence of the Lord (2 Thessalonians 1:9). And “they will not escape” is emphatic: by no means.

As labour pains. Labour is sudden in its onset, but not unexpected: the woman has known for months that it is coming. So with the day: its timing is unknown, its coming certain. And labour ends in a birth; the pains of the end precede a new creation (Romans 8:22). Paul does not develop this here, but his picture holds a hope the slogan never had.

Another king, Jesus. The mob that dragged Jason before the city rulers charged the believers with saying that “there is another king, Jesus” (Acts 17:7). Rome offered peace won by the sword; Christ made peace by the blood of his cross (Colossians 1:20), taking on himself the ruin this verse describes. His is the only peace and security still standing on the day of the Lord.

Where do I find false security in my own life? Wherever you feel safe without God: savings, health, career, reputation, a country’s stability, even a past religious experience you no longer live by. None is wrong to have; all are wrong to rest on. The only security that survives the day of the Lord is being in Christ.

Is this destruction really eternal? Is hell real? Yes. The destruction of the day of the Lord is not a temporary trouble but final ruin, described elsewhere as eternal destruction away from the presence of the Lord (2 Thessalonians 1:9) and as conscious, unending punishment (Matthew 25:46; Revelation 14:11). Jesus spoke of it more than anyone. It is taught not to frighten Christians, who are not destined for wrath (v. 9), but to wake the sleeping while there is time, and to show us what Christ saved us from.

Uncertain wording. Whether “peace and security” (eirēnē kai asphaleia) quotes an actual Roman slogan is not certain. Both ideas were constantly claimed for Roman rule, and the pair was probably close to a familiar boast, but Paul may simply be echoing the false prophets’ “Peace, peace”. Either way the meaning stands: ruin comes on people sure they are safe.
verseByVerse.note: “Peace and security” may echo the boasts of the Roman order.

parallels.desc: Peace, peace, when there is no peace

verseByVerse.quote: But you are not in darkness, brothers, for that day to surprise you like a thief. For you are all children of light, children of the day. We are not of the night or of the darkness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers will not be taken by surprise, because they already belong to the light and the day. They will not avoid the day, but it will not ambush them.

But you. Paul turns from the people saying “peace and security” to the church. A thief is a problem for the household that is asleep, not for a house with its lights on.

Children of light. In Hebrew speech a “son of” something belongs to it and is marked by it: children of light are people whose nature is light (Ephesians 5:8). Once they loved the dark and hid from God; now, with new hearts, they love what is true and want their deeds seen as done in God (John 3:19–21). And “all” matters: not only the mature or the leaders, but every believer, including the fainthearted and the weak of verse 14. Notice too that Paul tells them who they are before any command: not stay awake and you will be children of light, but you are children of light, therefore stay awake.

Believe in the light. The phrase comes from Jesus: “While you have the light, believe in the light, that you may become sons of light” (John 12:36; 8:12). The light is not a moral atmosphere but a Person, and they became his by believing in him; so Paul, a believer too, moves at once from “you” to “we”.

He entered our night. God is light, and in him is no darkness at all. Yet at noon on the day Jesus died, darkness came over all the land, and he was forsaken in it, so that children of the night could be called children of the day. Glory to the Son, who entered our night so that we could belong to his morning.

How did I become a child of light? By God’s act. God, “who said, ‘Let light shine out of darkness,’ has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6). He delivered us from the domain of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of his beloved Son (Colossians 1:13). You did not climb into the light; the light came to you, and every believer is there by the same grace.

I still do things that belong to the darkness. Am I really a child of light? If you trust Christ, yes. Children of light still sin, but they can no longer be at home in the night. The sign is not sinlessness but what you do with sin: hate it, confess it, turn from it (1 John 1:7–9). When you stumble, remember whose child you are and walk back toward the light.

verseByVerse.quote: So then let us not sleep, as others do, but let us keep awake and be sober. For those who sleep, sleep at night, and those who get drunk, are drunk at night.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because believers belong to the day, they must not drift into spiritual sleep but stay alert and clear-headed.

Let us not sleep. This sleep is not the tender word for the Christian dead (4:13–15) but spiritual carelessness. And it is “let us”: Paul does not consider himself immune.

Keep awake. Grēgoreō is the watchman’s word, and Jesus’ own: the doorkeeper stays awake because no one knows whether the master will come in the evening, at midnight, at cockcrow or in the morning (Mark 13:33–37), the four watches of the night. Christian wakefulness is not nervous vigilance but a servant listening for the footstep of a master he loves (John 14:3).

Be sober. Nēphō: clear-headed, in possession of your judgment, able to see what is actually there. Sobriety is not solemnity: this letter commands rejoicing ten verses later. It is knowing what will pass and what will last, and not being talked into confusing them.

At night. In the ancient city the night belonged to sleeping and carousing (Romans 13:12–13). Moral drowsiness in a Christian is like a man asleep in the street at noon: not a threat, but a life that does not fit the day he belongs to.

He kept watch when we could not. The same word describes the disciples in Gethsemane, who failed at it. There the Lord Jesus stayed awake for them, sweating in prayer while they dozed. He kept watch when we could not, and now he keeps watch over us.

What does spiritual sleep look like in an ordinary Christian? Rarely rebellion; usually drift: prayer occasional, the Bible unopened for weeks, church attended without attention, sins no longer noticed, eternity forgotten, the heart crowded with screens and schedules. The sleeper does not feel asleep, which is why we need one another to notice and wake each other up.

Does “be sober” forbid alcohol? No. Wine is a gift that gladdens the heart (Psalm 104:15), and Jesus made it; Scripture forbids drunkenness (Ephesians 5:18), and here uses it as a picture of a dulled mind. Some Christians abstain, for their own sake or for others, and that is a wise freedom. But let nothing, alcohol, entertainment, busyness or anxiety, cloud your judgment about what matters most.

verseByVerse.quote: But since we belong to the day, let us be sober, having put on the breastplate of faith and love, and for a helmet the hope of salvation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christians stay alert by putting on faith, love and hope, the armour God gives for the night watch. Sobriety comes not by trying harder to concentrate, but by getting dressed.

The breastplate of faith and love. The picture is a soldier on watch, drawn from Isaiah, where the LORD puts on righteousness as a breastplate and a helmet of salvation (Isaiah 59:17). The armour is faith, love and hope, the three that opened the letter (1:3), and faith and love cover the chest.

For a helmet the hope of salvation. Hope guards the head: it keeps you thinking straight. A church that loses hold of its hope cannot think clearly about the present, as had happened when their friends died. And this armour is all for protection: it keeps them standing until the day comes.

The armour the Redeemer wore. In Isaiah the LORD arms himself because he sees no one to intervene, and the passage ends with the promise that a Redeemer will come to Zion (Isaiah 59:16–20; Romans 11:26). The armour was first worn by Christ, who came to save, alone; believers wear the gear of a victory already won.

He went into battle stripped. Yet the Lord who arms his people went into his own battle stripped. For our helmet he wore thorns; for our breastplate his side was opened by a spear. He took the blows unguarded so that faith, love and hope could cover us through the night.

What does it mean to put on faith, love and hope in practice? Take hold of them deliberately each day, as a soldier straps on armour before the watch. Put on faith by recalling God’s promises and trusting them in today’s decisions. Put on love by deciding, before you meet people, to seek their good. Put on hope by setting your mind on Christ’s return, especially when discouragement starts to talk. Scripture, prayer and the fellowship of the church are where the armour is kept.

Is the hope of salvation certain, or might I lose it? Certain, because it rests on God’s appointment, as the next verse says: “God has not destined us for wrath, but to obtain salvation”. Biblical hope is not a “maybe” but sure, though not yet seen (Romans 8:24–25); it is a helmet because it holds when you are struck. If you are in Christ, your future salvation is as secure as his resurrection.

parallels.desc: righteousness as a breastplate, and a helmet of salvation

verseByVerse.quote: For God has not destined us for wrath, but to obtain salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ, who died for us so that whether we are awake or asleep we might live with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers can face the day without fear, because God has appointed them to salvation, won by Christ who died in their place. Whether they are alive or dead when he comes, they will live with him.

Not destined for wrath. Here is the ground under everything, answering the fear raised by talk of wrath since 1:10. The verb (tithēmi) means to appoint: God decided in advance on salvation for his people, not wrath, and not for anything they had done. This is election again, God’s choosing of his people (1:4; 2 Thessalonians 2:13).

To obtain salvation. To obtain is a word for coming into possession, as an heir comes into an estate: they are not hoping to be spared; they are on their way to collect.

Who died for us. Here is how: the only place in this letter where Paul says directly that Christ died as our substitute. “For us” (hyper hēmōn) means on our behalf and in our place. They escape wrath not because God overlooks sin, but because Christ stood where they stood and bore it himself (Romans 3:25; 1 John 2:2). For those who belong to him there is no wrath left to fall: no condemnation, no wrath stored up, no case pending.

Awake or asleep. Here “awake” means alive and “asleep” dead when Christ returns (4:13–18), not the watching and sleeping of verse 6, tying the two chapters together. Paul does not promise they will be alive at the coming, and in fact every one of them died; the promise is that either way they will live with him.

Why did Christ have to die for us? Could God not simply forgive? Forgiveness is free to us but not cheap. Sin is a real offence against a holy God, and a just judge cannot ignore it (Exodus 34:7). The wonder of the gospel is that God himself, in his Son, took the penalty, so that he is both just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (Romans 3:25–26).

How do I know I am destined for salvation and not wrath? Not by peering into God’s decrees but by looking to Christ. If you trust him who died for us, this verse is about you. Those God appointed to salvation he calls to faith (Romans 8:30), and faith is the sign of the appointment. If you are afraid, look not first at your feelings or your record but at the cross, where the wrath fell on him, and rest there.

Where Christians differ: not destined for wrath. Does this mean the church will be taken away before a future tribulation? Pretribulational Christians argue so from this verse, out of a real concern to honour God’s promise. This commentary’s view: The wrath here is God’s final judgment on the ungodly, from which Christ’s death saves believers (1:10; Romans 5:9). It does not promise exemption from suffering or persecution before the end; the Thessalonians were already suffering (3:3). Believers will be delivered from God’s wrath, not from all tribulation (John 16:33; Acts 14:22).

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore encourage one another and build one another up, just as you are doing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers are to keep strengthening one another with this hope, as they are already doing.

Encourage one another. For the second time (see 4:18) Paul ends a passage about the last day by telling them to speak to each other. The encouragement he means is not general cheerfulness but the sentence he has just written: Christ died for us so that, awake or asleep, we will live with him. To remind another believer of that is to set him again on Christ, the one foundation (1 Corinthians 3:11).

Build one another up. Build up (oikodomeō) is the word for constructing a building, which older Bibles translate “edify”. The Lord Jesus builds his church with living stones and uses our words of encouragement as his tools, and it is “one another”: ordinary members, not only the leaders of verse 12.

Just as you are doing. As before (4:1, 10), Paul ends graciously: he names the good they are already doing and asks for more of it. That is harder than criticism, and a good deal more effective.

How do I build someone up if I am not a teacher? With ordinary words, aimed well. Tell someone specifically where you see God’s grace in them. Share a verse that helped you this week, or remind a discouraged friend of a promise. Ask how you can pray, do it, and tell them you did. Thank someone for serving. Building up usually happens a sentence at a time, and anyone who loves Christ and his people can do it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A church waiting for its Lord lives as a family under his care. Its members honour the leaders who work hard among them and keep peace with one another (vv. 12–13); they give the idle, the fainthearted and the weak each what he needs, patiently (v. 14); they refuse revenge and pursue good (v. 15). Their life with God is joy, prayer and thanks in every circumstance (vv. 16–18), and their life with the Spirit is open but discerning: never quenching him, never despising prophecy, testing everything, keeping the good and shunning every form of evil (vv. 19–22).
verseByVerse.theology:
Discernment instead of either extreme

Verses 19–22 refuse both easy positions and ask for testing (see the note on vv. 19–22).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A congregation only months old already had leaders, honoured “because of their work” (v. 13).

Now: Verse 14 asks every member, not only leaders, to read the person in front of them before deciding whether to warn, encourage or hold up.

verseByVerse.quote: We ask you, brothers, to respect those who labor among you and are over you in the Lord and admonish you, and to esteem them very highly in love because of their work. Be at peace among yourselves.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The church is to value and love the leaders who work hard among them, because of their work, and to keep peace with one another.

Those who labour among you. Three descriptions of the same people, one job seen from three sides: church leaders, probably the elders, though the word is not used. They labour (kopiaō, work to the point of weariness, 1:3); they are over you (proistēmi, to lead, and also to care for); and they admonish (noutheteō, correction meant to change someone).

How young this was. This church was months old and already had recognised leaders, described by their work, not a title. The first thing owed them is respect, literally “to know” them: to notice who is doing the work and value it.

Why say this here. These leaders were themselves converts of a few months, with no apostle’s standing, and part of their work was telling the idle to get back to work (4:11). People corrected by their equals are quick to resent it, so Paul puts his own authority behind them before asking the whole church to do the same (v. 14).

Esteem them very highly. Paul piles up words for “very” again (hyperekperissou, beyond all measure, 3:10). The reason is not their office, gifts or personality, but their work. And in love, not merely as duty: a congregation that grasps what the work costs, the broken nights, the conversation nobody wants to have, finds esteem easier to give.

Over you in the Lord. They lead under Christ and answer to him, not lords over the flock (1 Peter 5:3) but servants of the one who came not to be served but to serve (Mark 10:44–45). A church that honours its faithful leaders is honouring Christ’s gift, and a leader who domineers has forgotten whose flock it is.

Be at peace among yourselves. Paul probably adds a safeguard: esteem them, but not so highly that you form parties around them. Without peace among the members, no one can lead at all.

How do we keep the peace? Church peace is not the absence of disagreement but people who disagree staying joined. Christ made that possible before he commanded it: “he himself is our peace,” and by his cross he has broken down “the dividing wall of hostility” (Ephesians 2:14). We do not build that unity; we keep it (Ephesians 4:3). In practice: Go, do not gossip: take a grievance to the person, not to a third party (Matthew 18:15). Overlook what you can: love covers a multitude of sins (1 Peter 4:8). Refuse to form a party: do not gather people around a favourite leader or a grudge. Own your part quickly: say “I was wrong” without adding “but”. Come to the Lord’s Table together: it is hard to keep a feud alive with someone beside whom you receive the same bread. The one who forgave you everything is the one who asks this of you.

What if my church leaders get things wrong? They will, being sinners like you; honour does not mean pretending otherwise. Pray for them first. Let matters of preference go graciously. Take a real concern to them privately and humbly (Matthew 18:15). If there is serious sin or false teaching, Scripture gives a careful process (1 Timothy 5:19–20). And abuse of any kind must never be covered up: it is to be brought into the light and, where it is a crime, reported, whoever the leader is. Respect for leaders never means silence about harm.

How do I actually show esteem to my pastor and elders? Pray for them by name. Tell them specifically when their ministry has helped you. Receive their teaching and admonition without resentment (Hebrews 13:17), and do not gossip about them. Support them practically, including generously providing for those who teach (1 Timothy 5:17–18; Galatians 6:6). Care for their families, and turn up and serve. A leader who knows he is loved can bear far more.

verseByVerse.quote: And we urge you, brothers, admonish the idle, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak, be patient with them all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every member is to give each struggling believer what he actually needs, and to be patient with them all. Paul speaks to all the brothers, not just the leaders.

Admonish the idle. This is the problem of 4:11 (2 Thessalonians 3:6–12; on the word, see the box below). The idle need not sympathy but to be told to get back to work.

Encourage the fainthearted. Literally small-souled (oligopsychoi): those whose courage has run low, and a church burying friends had plenty. Comfort them.

Help the weak. To help (antechomai) means to hold on to, to support, like taking someone’s arm. The weak, in faith, conscience, body or circumstance, need not advice but someone bearing some of the weight.

Three troubles, three cures. The wrong response does damage. The lazy man comforted stays lazy; the frightened man rebuked despairs; the weak man told to try harder simply falls over. Wise care finds out what is wrong before it treats.

Be patient with them all. Long-tempered, slow to boil (makrothymeō). The idle will not start, the fainthearted will not be reassured, the weak will need holding up again next week. Patience, the Spirit’s fruit (Galatians 5:22), keeps you doing the right thing the eleventh time.

Each one as the Lord treated them. This is no technique; it is how the Lord Jesus dealt with people. He warned the careless plainly, as in the parable of the servant who buried his master’s money and blamed his fear (Matthew 25:24–27). To terrified men in a boat at night he said, “Take heart; it is I. Do not be afraid” (Matthew 14:27). And when Peter began to sink, Jesus immediately reached out his hand and took hold of him (Matthew 14:31), the very gesture the word “help” describes. A church that warns, encourages and holds up the weak is doing to one another what its Lord does for each of them.

He was patient with us first. He was patient with us first: with the idle, with fainthearted disciples who ran, with weak ones who could not keep awake one hour. In Paul, the foremost of sinners, Christ Jesus displayed his perfect patience (1 Timothy 1:16), and every patient word we give a struggling brother is drawn from that supply.

How do I know which one a person needs? Listen before you speak, and ask questions: will they not, can they not, or are they afraid? Many people are a mixture, and needs change with seasons. Pray for wisdom (James 1:5), take time to know people, and change your approach when you see you have misjudged.

What if I am the fainthearted or the weak one? Then this verse tells your church to care for you, and there is no shame in receiving it. Tell someone honestly how you are, and let others hold your arm; you need not pretend to be strong to belong. The Lord does not break a bruised reed or quench a smouldering wick (Isaiah 42:3), and he has told his people to treat you the same way.

Uncertain wording. The word translated “idle” (ataktoi) first described soldiers out of rank, so it could mean “disorderly” or “unruly” in general, as older versions have it; in everyday use it also described people who shirked work. The parallel in 2 Thessalonians 3:6–12, where the disorderly are those who will not work, makes “idle” the likely meaning; refusing to work was itself a breaking of rank.
verseByVerse.note: “Idle” may mean those who had stopped working, perhaps expecting the Lord’s imminent return.

verseByVerse.quote: See that no one repays anyone evil for evil, but always seek to do good to one another and to everyone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christians must never take revenge, but keep pursuing good for fellow believers and for everyone else.

See that no one repays. Stopping revenge is the whole church’s business (Romans 12:17; 1 Peter 3:9). This was written not for comfortable people but for believers driven from families and squeezed out of trades, with genuine grievances against identifiable neighbours.

Always seek to do good. To seek (diōkō) means to chase after, the same word used for persecuting. Pursued with evil, they were to pursue others with good.

What makes it possible. The Lord is an avenger (4:6), so the wronged Christian need not secure justice himself. And these people are not destined for wrath (5:9): they have received the mercy they are now asked to show. Refusing revenge is not pretending the wrong did not happen, but handing it to the Judge who will deal with it justly.

The persecutor who was pursued. Paul had himself been an enemy who was loved (Luke 6:27–28). He once persecuted the church (the same verb), and the risen Christ met him asking, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4). The Lord chased his enemy down with mercy and made him an apostle. He repaid our evil with good, and his good was a cross.

Does doing good to someone who hurt me mean I must trust them or stay near them? No. Doing good is not giving access. You can refuse revenge, pray for someone and wish them well while keeping a safe distance, especially where there has been abuse or danger. Forgiveness releases the debt to God; trust is rebuilt only where there is real repentance and change, and sometimes not at all. Reporting a crime or seeking protection is not repaying evil; it is seeking justice by the means God has given.

What does doing good look like toward someone I resent? Small, concrete things. Speak of them fairly; refuse to join in mockery; pray for their blessing, meaning it as far as you can; help them in need; answer a sharp word gently. Feelings may lag, but deeds of good often lead the heart, and they always honour Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks in all circumstances; for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s will for his people is constant joy, constant prayer and thanks in every circumstance, a life resting on him rather than on how things are going.

Rejoice always. Two words in Greek, and no call to pretend. Joy here is what it was in 1:6, given by the Holy Spirit in much affliction, and always possible because it rests on the Lord, not on circumstances (Philippians 4:4).

Pray without ceasing. Without ceasing (adialeiptōs) could describe a persistent cough, something that keeps recurring. Paul means a line to God that is never closed: regular times of prayer, and between them a heart that keeps turning to him, who is always listening and always good.

Give thanks in all circumstances. In all circumstances, not for all circumstances. No one is asked to be grateful for a death or a betrayal, but to keep giving thanks inside such things, because God’s goodness does not pause and he is at work in all of them (Romans 8:28).

The will of God in Christ Jesus. The letter’s second plain statement of God’s will; the first was their sanctification (4:3). The three commands belong together: joy without prayer becomes shallow optimism; prayer without thanksgiving becomes a list of complaints; thanksgiving without joy becomes a duty.

On the night he was betrayed. And all of it is “in Christ Jesus”. Paul knew of thanks given in the darkest hour there has ever been: on the night when he was betrayed the Lord Jesus took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it (1 Corinthians 11:23–24). He gave thanks with the cross hours away, over bread that meant his own body. This will of God is not an ideal we strain toward alone but the life of the Son, who rejoiced, prayed and gave thanks perfectly, in our place, and now lives it out by his Spirit in those joined to him. For his sake our faltering prayers and thanks are accepted, and our thanks in hard places is an echo of his.

How can I rejoice when I am grieving or depressed? Christian joy is not a happy mood; it can coexist with tears and even with dark seasons of the mind. The psalms of lament are full of sorrow, yet most still turn toward God and end with trust. Joy at its root is the settled fact that Christ is yours and you are his, and you can hold on to that even when you cannot feel it. If you are depressed, talk to your pastor and seek out a biblical counsellor, who will also ask you to have a medical check-up; if medicine is needed, taking it is no failure of faith. If you ever think of ending your life, tell someone and get help that same day. And let others rejoice and pray on your behalf until joy returns.

How do I pray without ceasing in a busy life? Keep regular times of prayer, morning and evening if you can. Then attach short prayers to ordinary moments: waking, meals, the commute, the start of a meeting, a hard email, a piece of good news. Turn worries into requests as they arise, and pleasures into thanks, until turning to God becomes a reflex.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not quench the Spirit. Do not despise prophecies, but test everything; hold fast what is good. Abstain from every form of evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The church must neither smother the Spirit’s work nor swallow every claim made in his name, but test everything, keep the good and reject evil in every form.

Do not quench the Spirit. The first of five short commands about the Spirit’s work in the gathered church. The verb (sbennymi) means to put out a fire, and the Spirit came at Pentecost in tongues “as of fire” (Acts 2:3). A fire dies when smothered or not fed, so we quench the Spirit by sin, by neglect, or by suppressing his work.

Do not despise prophecies. Some in Thessalonica apparently scorned prophecy, words from the Spirit spoken in the gathered church. One can see why: the second letter deals with a claimed message that the day of the Lord had already come (2 Thessalonians 2:2), and after that the instinct is to shut all prophecy down.

Test everything. Paul refuses that instinct: neither believing nor dismissing everything, but testing: dokimazō, the word of 2:4, used of proving metal genuine (1 John 4:1). Now that the apostolic word stands complete in Scripture, every claim to speak for God is tested against it.

Hold fast what is good. Keep what passes the test: discernment that only ever rejects has failed at half its job. Drop whatever proves bad, whatever authority was claimed for it; abstain from evil in every shape it takes (on the wording of verse 22, see the box below).

What the Spirit always says. The Spirit always points to the same person. Jesus said of him, “He will glorify me” (John 16:14). So the New Testament’s tests turn on Christ (1 Corinthians 12:3; 1 John 4:2). A word that makes much of the speaker or the experience, and little of the crucified and risen Lord, has already failed.

Open, and awake. The five commands refuse both easy positions: a church so afraid of disorder that it quenches the Spirit, or so afraid of quenching him that it swallows anything. Paul asks for the harder combination.

How might a cessationist church quench the Spirit? By treating the Bible as a museum piece rather than God’s living voice; by preaching without prayer; by resisting conviction of sin; by stifling the gifts he does give, such as teaching, encouragement, mercy and service; or by a coldness that never expects God to change anyone. Cessationism rightly guards the closed canon; it must never become an excuse for spiritual deadness.

How do I keep from quenching the Spirit in my own life? The Spirit’s fuel is Christ, whom he makes known to us (John 16:14–15), so the ordinary ways are the right ones. Keep his word open: the Spirit speaks through Scripture, and a Bible left shut is a fire left unfed. Obey promptly: when conscience stirs you to make a call or put something right, do it today. Confess quickly: unconfessed sin smothers the flame, and Christ’s blood is always the way back (1 John 1:9). Stay near the fire: gather with his people, where the Spirit gives his gifts for the common good (1 Corinthians 12:7). And take heart: the Spirit is not a guest who leaves at the first slight; he has sealed you for the day of redemption (Ephesians 4:30), and he will finish what he began.

What if someone tells me God gave them a word for me? Listen respectfully, then test it by Scripture. If it contradicts the Bible, reject it, however sincere the speaker. If it is a biblical truth applied, such as a promise recalled or a warning against a sin Scripture names, receive it as good counsel, but its authority comes from Scripture, not from the claim. Make no major decision on such words alone; ask wise, mature believers and your pastors. God’s will for you is found in his written word, obeyed wisely and prayerfully.

Uncertain wording. The word in verse 22 (eidos) can mean “appearance” or “form, kind”. The KJV’s “abstain from all appearance of evil” is often taken to mean avoiding anything that might look wrong to others. The ESV’s “every form of evil” is the likelier rendering: shun evil in every shape it takes, rather than live by other people’s impressions. Avoiding needless offence is wise, but it is not the point here.

Where Christians differ: prophecy today. Does this mean prophecy continues today? Continuationist Christians (who believe all the New Testament gifts continue) see here a command to welcome prophecy now, and many are wise and godly believers whose reasons deserve a hearing; some cessationists simply dismiss the passage. This commentary’s view: In the apostolic churches, before the New Testament was complete, prophecy was an active gift, and Paul commanded the church neither to despise nor accept it uncritically. With the completion of Scripture, revelatory prophecy has ceased (Ephesians 2:20; Hebrews 1:1–2). But the principles remain: do not quench the Spirit, who speaks through the word; test every teaching and claim by Scripture; hold to what is good. These apply to preaching, teaching and every claim of spiritual guidance today. This view is held with charity toward continuationist brothers and sisters.

verseByVerse.ref: 5:23–28 – Kept Blameless, and the Last Word
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: What Paul has commanded, only God can produce, so the letter ends in prayer and promise. Paul asks the God of peace to make them holy through and through and keep them blameless until Christ comes, and assures them that the faithful God who calls them will do it (vv. 23–24). He asks for their prayers, greets the whole family, binds them to have the letter read to everyone (vv. 25–27), and leaves them with the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ (v. 28).
verseByVerse.theology:
Whole persons, and who does the keeping

“Spirit and soul and body” (v. 23) is a way of saying the whole of you, and they are to be kept by the God who calls them and is faithful (v. 24).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The oath of verse 27 ensured the letter reached every believer, the illiterate included.

Now: The holy kiss for all the brothers (v. 26) quietly undoes rank: you cannot greet someone as family every week and go on regarding him as beneath you.

verseByVerse.quote: Now may the God of peace himself sanctify you completely, and may your whole spirit and soul and body be kept blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. He who calls you is faithful; he will surely do it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul prays that God will make believers holy through and through and keep them blameless until Christ comes, and he promises that the faithful God will do it.

The God of peace himself. The letter turns to prayer, echoing the close of chapter 3 (3:13), because what Paul has commanded only God can produce. The God of peace makes peace with sinners through the blood of his Son. “Himself”: having told them to be holy, to work, to love, to stay awake, Paul now prays. And the holiness he asks for is complete: holoteleis, through and through, right to the finish.

Spirit and soul and body. Is a person made of three parts or two (see the box “Where Christians differ: spirit, soul and body” at the end of this note)? Scripture uses the two words side by side for the same thing (Luke 1:46–47), and Deuteronomy 6:5 piles up words similarly, love the LORD with all your heart and soul and might, which nobody takes as a list of parts. It is a way of saying the whole of you.

Kept blameless. “Be kept” (tēreō, guarded) is passive: it is something done to them. They are not keeping themselves; someone is keeping them, which is the difference between exhaustion and rest. Like every chapter of the letter, this one ends with Christ’s coming.

Blameless before whom? How can anyone who knows his own heart be blameless when the Lord Jesus comes? Paul answers elsewhere: Christ has reconciled us in his body of flesh by his death, in order to present us holy and blameless and above reproach before him (Colossians 1:22). The one before whom we must stand is the one who made us fit to stand. God counts us blameless now through his death, and his Spirit makes us so, until the day we see him and are made like him (1 John 3:2).

He will surely do it. Then the prayer becomes a promise. The calling is present tense, as in 2:12: he goes on calling. The guarantee is not their staying power but his character: he does not begin what he will not finish (Philippians 1:6; 1 Corinthians 1:8–9). He kept every promise from Abraham to the empty tomb, and he will keep this one.

If God will do it, why should I make any effort? Because God sanctifies us through our effort, not instead of it. Paul can say in one breath, “work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you, both to will and to work” (Philippians 2:12–13). His promise is not a reason to stop fighting sin but the reason the fight is not hopeless: you strive because he is at work, and rest because the outcome depends on him. Effort without the promise despairs; the promise without effort misreads it.

Does my body matter to God as much as my soul? Yes: Paul prays for the body to be kept blameless too. God made the body, the Son took one, the Spirit dwells in it, and it will be raised. So what you do with it, sexual purity, honest work, care for health, rest, the use of eyes, hands and tongue, is part of your holiness. Christianity does not despise the physical; it sanctifies it.

In everyday life. Discouraged at how slowly you change? Read verse 24 aloud: “He who calls you is faithful; he will surely do it.” Then take the next small step of obedience in front of you, and leave the finishing to him.

Where Christians differ: spirit, soul and body. Some (trichotomists) take this to mean humans have three distinct parts: spirit, soul and body. Others (dichotomists) hold two: body and soul (or spirit). This commentary’s view: Scripture usually describes humans as body and soul, or body and spirit, using soul and spirit interchangeably (Matthew 10:28; 1 Corinthians 7:34; Ecclesiastes 12:7). Paul here stresses the whole person, every aspect, not giving a technical anatomy. The majority Reformed view is that humans are a unity of body and soul (Westminster Larger Catechism Q. 17; Westminster 4.2).

Where Christians differ: entire sanctification. Some in the Wesleyan tradition, a tradition rich in earnest pursuit of holiness, take this verse to teach that believers can be sanctified entirely in this life, free from sin. This commentary’s view: Paul prays for complete sanctification, and God will accomplish it, at the coming of Christ. In this life, believers grow in holiness but remain sinners (1 John 1:8). Sanctification is complete at glorification (Philippians 3:12), as the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession teach (Westminster 13.2; 1689 13.2).

verseByVerse.quote: Brothers, pray for us. Greet all the brothers with a holy kiss. I put you under oath before the Lord to have this letter read to all the brothers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul asks for their prayers, sends his love to the whole family, and insists that every member hear the letter.

Brothers, pray for us. The apostle who prays for them night and day (3:10) asks for their prayers: mutual intercession is the life of the church.

A holy kiss. The kiss on the cheek was an ordinary greeting between family and close friends, and it became the family greeting of the early church (Romans 16:16). What is not ordinary is the range: all the brothers. In a room containing slaves and masters, Jews and Greeks, the householder and the day labourer, that instruction breaks down rank. “Holy” sets it apart from the ordinary social kiss.

Read to all the brothers. The verb is strong, putting them under solemn oath, most probably because of the word “all”. Letters were read aloud; many believers could not read. Paul wants nobody left out: not the slaves who might miss a meeting, not the fainthearted and the weak he has just named.

Before the Lord. The oath is sworn by the Lord, which in this letter almost always means Jesus. They had received Paul’s preaching as the word of God (2:13), and whoever hears Christ’s messengers hears him (Luke 10:16). So the letter is to be read to the whole assembly, as the Scriptures were read in the synagogue (Colossians 4:16). To keep it from any of them would be to stand between the Shepherd and his sheep.

Must Christians greet one another with a kiss today? The command is for a warm, sincere greeting in the form one’s culture uses: a kiss where it carries that meaning, elsewhere a handshake or an embrace. What matters is that no one is left ungreeted, and that the greeting is pure and genuine.

How should I pray for my pastor and for missionaries? Pray as Paul asked elsewhere: that the word of the Lord may speed ahead and be honoured, that they may be delivered from wicked people (2 Thessalonians 3:1–2), that doors would open for the gospel and they would speak it clearly (Colossians 4:3–4), and that they would be bold (Ephesians 6:19–20). Pray for their holiness, families, health and joy. Ask what they need prayer for, and tell them you prayed.

Textual note. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, read all the holy brothers; the earliest lack “holy”, so most modern Bibles omit it.
verseByVerse.note: The holy kiss was the family greeting of the early church.

verseByVerse.quote: The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The letter’s last word is not a command but a gift: the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, staying with them.

Grace to close. The letter opened with grace (1:1) and closes with it. Between them stand persecution, burials, slander answered and hard commands, all of it inside grace. The greeting was “Grace to you”: grace arriving. Here grace is to “be with you”: grace staying, accompanying them into whatever came next. Paul could not come himself; what he can send is this.

What came next. It was not easy. They would remain a small, pressured minority in a proud Roman city, and within months, probably, Paul would write again because confusion about the Lord’s coming had grown. His last word is what would still be true through all of it.

Grace with a name. Grace has a name and a history: “though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor” (2 Corinthians 8:9). A letter that ends with grace ends with him, going with them into whatever comes. And his grace has not grown thin with use: it was poured out at the cross, carried the Thessalonians through persecution and grief, and will bring his people home on the day of his coming.

What is grace, exactly? Grace is God’s free, undeserved favour toward sinners in Christ, and his power at work in them. It is favour: God treats us not as our sins deserve but as his Son deserves. And it is power: the same grace that forgives also changes, strengthens and keeps (2 Corinthians 12:9; Titus 2:11–12). He bought it at the cross and gives it from the throne. Every command in this letter is obeyed by it, and every promise kept by it.

5.text: <sup>1</sup>Now concerning the times and the seasons, brothers, you have no need to have anything written to you.<sup>2</sup>For you yourselves are fully aware that the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night.<sup>3</sup>While people are saying, "There is peace and security," then sudden destruction will come upon them as labor pains come upon a pregnant woman, and they will not escape.<sup>4</sup>But you are not in darkness, brothers, for that day to surprise you like a thief.<sup>5</sup>For you are all children of light, children of the day. We are not of the night or of the darkness.<sup>6</sup>So then let us not sleep, as others do, but let us keep awake and be sober.<sup>7</sup>For those who sleep, sleep at night, and those who get drunk, are drunk at night.<sup>8</sup>But since we belong to the day, let us be sober, having put on the breastplate of faith and love, and for a helmet the hope of salvation.<sup>9</sup>For God has not destined us for wrath, but to obtain salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ,<sup>10</sup>who died for us so that whether we are awake or asleep we might live with him.<sup>11</sup>Therefore encourage one another and build one another up, just as you are doing.<sup>12</sup>We ask you, brothers, to respect those who labor among you and are over you in the Lord and admonish you,<sup>13</sup>and to esteem them very highly in love because of their work. Be at peace among yourselves.<sup>14</sup>And we urge you, brothers, admonish the idle, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak, be patient with them all.<sup>15</sup>See that no one repays anyone evil for evil, but always seek to do good to one another and to everyone.<sup>16</sup>Rejoice always,<sup>17</sup>pray without ceasing,<sup>18</sup>give thanks in all circumstances; for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you.<sup>19</sup>Do not quench the Spirit.<sup>20</sup>Do not despise prophecies,<sup>21</sup>but test everything; hold fast what is good.<sup>22</sup>Abstain from every form of evil.<sup>23</sup>Now may the God of peace himself sanctify you completely, and may your whole spirit and soul and body be kept blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.<sup>24</sup>He who calls you is faithful; he will surely do it.<sup>25</sup>Brothers, pray for us.<sup>26</sup>Greet all the brothers with a holy kiss.<sup>27</sup>I put you under oath before the Lord to have this letter read to all the brothers.<sup>28</sup>The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.

keyVerse.quote: For God has not destined us for wrath, but to obtain salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ,
keyVerse.note: This is the ground under the whole chapter. The day of the Lord will bring sudden ruin, yet believers can wait for it awake and unafraid, because God has already decided their future and Christ has already borne the wrath in their place (v. 10). Every command that follows, from encouraging one another to giving thanks in all circumstances, is the life of people who know they are on their way to salvation.

5.reflection:
Paul refuses to give a date for the Lord’s coming (vv. 1–2) but insists on readiness. Why are people drawn either to setting dates or to forgetting Christ’s return altogether, and what would being ready look like in an ordinary week?

Verses 6–8 contrast spiritual sleep with the armour of faith, love and hope. Where do you notice drift in your own life, and how can we help one another stay awake?

Verse 14 names the idle, the fainthearted and the weak, each needing something different. Which have you been, and what helped you? How can we get better at seeing which a person needs?

Verse 24 says, “He who calls you is faithful; he will surely do it.” How does this promise, resting on Christ who died for us (vv. 9–10), change the way you face slow progress in holiness?
